_README: Explanations for correct answers, shown in study mode only. Keyed by question ID. 'src' names the authority, 'x' is the explanation (<150 words). Style: exam focused. Lead with the rule or principle that IS the answer, quote the decisive language, give a recall cue. Do not walk through why each distractor fails. Source priority: 47 CFR Part 97 > other FCC rules > ARRL > peer-reviewed engineering (IEEE/university) > third-party study sites as a last resort. Answers themselves are never modified by this file; extract.py asserts that.

E1A01.x: USB puts your energy above the displayed carrier frequency. Add the 3 kHz bandwidth to 14.348 and the signal reaches 14.351 MHz, while 20 meters stops at 14.350. That top 1 kHz falls outside the band, and §97.307(b) requires emissions to stay confined to the segment available to you.

E1A02.x: LSB places energy below the displayed frequency, so a 3 kHz signal extends 3 kHz down. To keep all of it inside, set the carrier at least 3 kHz above the lower edge. USB works the mirror image: stay 3 kHz below the upper edge.

E1A03.x: Data on 20 meters must sit below 14.150 MHz, and USB extends upward from the carrier. Subtract the 2.8 kHz bandwidth from 14.150 and you get 14.1472 MHz. Take the segment edge and back off by the bandwidth.

E1A04.x: The 75-meter phone segment starts at 3.600 MHz. An LSB signal on 3.601 spreads roughly 3 kHz downward, reaching about 3.598, which puts most of it below the edge. Being inside the band with your carrier is not enough when the sidebands are not.

E1A05.x: Section 97.5(a) requires the apparatus to be under the physical control of a person named in an amateur license grant or authorized for alien reciprocal operation. Vessel registry decides which rules apply; the licensing requirement itself does not change.

E1A06.x: On the four discrete 60-meter channels, phone, data and RTTY are offset 1.5 kHz below center so the suppressed-carrier signal lands centered in the channel. CW carries no sidebands, so it is transmitted right at the center frequency.

E1A07.x: Two limits apply on 2200 meters and the tighter one governs: 1.5 kW PEP at the transmitter, but only 1 watt EIRP radiated. Antennas at 137 kHz are so short compared with a wavelength that they radiate a tiny fraction of what you feed them.

E1A08.x: In a message forwarding system the control operator of the originating station is primarily accountable for a violation in the message. Section 97.219(c) protects intermediate forwarding stations that pass it along inadvertently. Accountability sits with whoever wrote it.

E1A09.x: On 630 meters the ceiling is 500 W PEP at the transmitter and 5 watts EIRP radiated. Pair it with the 2200-meter figure: 1 watt on 2200, 5 watts on 630, both EIRP.

E1A10.x: Installing and operating an amateur station aboard a ship or aircraft "must be approved by the master of the ship or pilot in command of the aircraft." Their authority over the vessel outranks your license. Section 97.11(b) adds that the station must be independent of the vessel's own radio gear.

E1A11.x: A US-registered vessel carries US jurisdiction with it into international waters, so any FCC-issued amateur license is sufficient. No endorsement, no maritime permit, and no foreign authorization is needed while you are aboard.

E1B01.x: The definition: "An emission, or frequencies outside the necessary bandwidth of a transmission, the level of which may be reduced without affecting the information being transmitted." That last clause is the test. If removing it costs you nothing, it was spurious.

E1B02.x: No non-phone emission may exceed the bandwidth of a communications quality phone signal of the same modulation type. On HF that benchmark is about 3 kHz, so digital voice and SSTV are held to the same width as an SSB conversation.

E1B03.x: A station within 1600 meters, which is 1 mile, of an FCC monitoring facility must protect it from harmful interference. Fail to do so and the FCC may impose operating restrictions on your station.

E1B04.x: Amateurs are secondary on 70 centimeters and must not cause harmful interference to the radiolocation service. If your repeater is the source, the obligation is immediate: cease operating or change the repeater so the interference stops.

E1B05.x: The National Radio Quiet Zone is a rectangle across Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia protecting the National Radio Astronomy Observatory at Green Bank. Its telescopes listen for signals far weaker than anything a transmitter nearby would leave intact.

E1B06.x: The 200-foot threshold is not the only trigger. A structure at or near a public use airport may require FAA notification and FCC registration under Part 17 at heights well below 200 feet, because the limit there follows the airport's glide slope.

E1B07.x: PRB-1 is the FCC's limited preemption of state and local zoning as it applies to amateur antenna structures. It reaches land use and zoning rules, not private deed restrictions or homeowner association covenants, which are contracts rather than government regulation.

E1B08.x: When your station interferes with domestic broadcast reception on receivers of good engineering design, the FCC may impose quiet hours: you avoid transmitting on the offending frequencies during specified times. The remedy restricts when and where you operate rather than shutting you down.

E1B09.x: Any FCC-licensed amateur station may operate under RACES rules once it is certified by the civil defense organization responsible for the area served. The license alone is not enough, and no separate class of station license exists for RACES.

E1B10.x: RACES operation uses the ordinary amateur allocations. Every frequency and emission authorized to the control operator by license class remains available, shared with the amateur service. There is no separate block of RACES-only spectrum.

E1B11.x: Local regulation must reasonably accommodate amateur service communications and represent the minimum practical regulation needed to serve the locality's legitimate purpose. Reasonable accommodation is the operative phrase, and it does not mean a jurisdiction has to permit any structure you want.

E1C01.x: All 60-meter emissions are limited to 2.8 kHz occupied bandwidth, data included. One figure covers every mode on the band, which matches the width of an ordinary SSB signal.

E1C02.x: International transmissions are "limited to communications incidental to the purposes of the amateur service and to remarks of a personal character." One sentence covering every DX contact you will ever make, and the answer restates it.

E1C03.x: After notifying the UTC you wait 30 days. If nothing comes back saying your station sits within 1 kilometer of a power line carrier system using those frequencies, you may operate. Silence after 30 days is your clearance.

E1C04.src: CITEL Inter-American Convention; FCC International Bureau
E1C04.x: The International Amateur Radio Permit comes out of the CITEL convention and lets US amateurs operate in participating countries across the Americas without applying for a separate license in each one. Think of IARP as the Western Hemisphere counterpart to CEPT.

E1C05.x: Section 97.115(c) bars third-party traffic under automatic control, "except a station transmitting a RTTY or data emission." Automated digital forwarding systems keep working; automated phone relay of third-party messages does not.

E1C06.x: Operating under CEPT abroad requires you to carry proof of your authority: your FCC license plus a copy of Public Notice DA 16-1048, which is the document establishing that US amateurs may use CEPT privileges. Carry both, because a foreign administration has no other way to verify you.

E1C07.x: Before operating on 2200 or 630 meters you notify the Utilities Technology Council of your call sign, the band or bands you intend to use, and the coordinates of your antenna's fixed location. The point is to check you are clear of power line carrier systems sharing those frequencies.

E1C08.x: A telecommand station must include provisions limiting transmission to no more than 3 minutes if the control link fails. Without it a stuck transmitter could hold a frequency indefinitely with nobody able to stop it.

E1C09.x: Below 29.0 MHz no angle-modulated emission may have a modulation index greater than 1 at the highest modulation frequency. Holding the index at 1.0 keeps the occupied bandwidth from expanding into neighboring HF signals.

E1C10.x: For transmitters installed after January 1, 2003, spurious emissions below 30 MHz must be at least 43 dB below the mean power of the fundamental. Above 30 MHz the requirement tightens to 60 dB, so keep the two figures paired.

E1C11.src: CEPT Recommendation T/R 61-01; FCC Public Notice DA 16-1048
E1C11.x: CEPT is the European arrangement that lets a US amateur operate in participating countries, and their amateurs operate here, without a separate license application. IARP does the same job in the Americas.

E1C12.x: The emission table authorizes phone across the whole 630-meter band. Very little voice happens there in practice because the band is 7 kHz wide and power is capped at 5 watts EIRP, but the rules permit it throughout.

E1D01.x: Definition, verbatim: "Telemetry. A one-way transmission of measurements at a distance from the measuring instrument." One-way and measurements are the two elements. Telemetry reports data outward; telecommand sends control the other direction.

E1D02.x: Section 97.211(b) permits a space telecommand station to "transmit special codes intended to obscure the meaning of telecommand messages." The reason is security: anyone able to decode the commands could take over the spacecraft.

E1D03.x: A space telecommand station is the ground station that commands the satellite, transmitting to "initiate, modify, or terminate functions" of a space station. Telecommand goes up and controls; telemetry comes down and reports.

E1D04.x: A balloon telemetry beacon is an amateur station like any other, so §97.119(a) applies in full and the call sign must go out. Nothing in the rules requires altitude, position or speed to be transmitted, however common those are in practice.

E1D05.x: Section 97.213(d) requires a photocopy of the station license and a label showing the name, address and telephone number of the licensee and at least one designated control operator, posted conspicuously at the station. Since every listed item appears in the rule, the inclusive answer is right.

E1D06.x: Model craft telecommand is capped at 1 watt. Section 97.215 also waives on-air identification for those transmissions, provided a label with your call sign and address is affixed to the transmitter.

E1D07.x: Space stations get 40, 20, 15 and 10 meters on HF, specifically the 7.0 to 7.1 MHz and 14.00 to 14.25 MHz segments plus the 17, 15, 12 and 10 meter bands. Below 40 meters nothing is allocated, since satellite work needs frequencies that pass through the ionosphere.

E1D08.x: On VHF only 2 meters carries a space station allocation, at 144 to 146 MHz. Note this is the lower half of the band only, not all of 144 to 148, which is why 145.8 to 146.0 shows up as a satellite subband in practice.

E1D09.x: Two UHF bands are authorized: 435 to 438 MHz on 70 centimeters and 2400 to 2450 MHz on 13 centimeters. The 435 MHz segment carries most amateur satellite downlinks you will actually hear.

E1D10.x: Eligibility comes from designation, not license class. Any amateur station designated by the space station licensee may act as its telecommand station, and the control operator then works within the privileges of the license held.

E1D11.x: Any amateur station may be an Earth station, and any class of operator may control one, within their own privileges. An Earth station is simply a ground station communicating through a satellite, which is what most operators are doing on the birds.

E1D12.x: One-way transmission is normally prohibited, but three station types are given explicit permission: space stations, beacons and telecommand stations. Each has a purpose that cannot work as a two-way exchange.

E1E01.x: Section 97.527 allows reimbursement for out-of-pocket expenses incurred "in preparing, processing, administering, or coordinating an examination." Actual costs only. VEs receive no payment for their time, and §97.509(e) makes charging beyond that a serious violation.

E1E02.x: All VECs must cooperate in maintaining one question pool per written element, each holding at least ten times the number of questions used on a single exam. The VECs own the pools jointly. The FCC does not write the questions.

E1E03.x: A VEC is an organization that has entered into a written agreement with the FCC to coordinate, prepare and administer amateur license examinations. The agreement with the Commission is what makes an organization a VEC.

E1E04.x: Accreditation is the VEC confirming that a candidate meets the FCC's requirements: correct license class, at least 18 years old, and never revoked or suspended. The VEC may also decline anyone it judges not competent or whose integrity is in question.

E1E05.x: On a failing grade the VE team returns the application document to the examinee and tells them the grade. Nothing goes to the VEC. The paperwork is theirs to keep, and they may test again the same day if the session allows it.

E1E06.x: Responsibility is individual, not collective. The rule states that the administering VEs are responsible for the proper conduct and necessary supervision of each examination, and each VE must observe the examinee throughout. No one gets to defer to the team lead.

E1E07.x: Section 97.511 requires each examinee to comply with the instructions given by the administering VEs. If a candidate will not, the VE terminates that examination immediately. There is no warning step written into the rules.

E1E08.x: A VE may not examine a spouse, child, grandchild, stepchild, parent, grandparent, stepparent, sibling, stepsibling, aunt, uncle, niece, nephew, or in-law. The list is long and specific, and the point is avoiding any appearance of favoritism.

E1E09.x: Fraudulent administration or certification may result in revocation of the VE's station license grant and suspension of the operator license grant. The penalty falls on the examiner's own license, which is what gives the volunteer system its teeth.

E1E10.x: After a successful examination the VEs submit the application document to the coordinating VEC according to that VEC's instructions. It goes to the VEC rather than straight to the FCC, and the VEC forwards it onward.

E1E11.x: Three VEs must certify both that the examinee is qualified for the license grant and that they themselves complied with the administering VE requirements. Three signatures, and they attest to their own conduct as well as the candidate's result.

E1F01.x: Spread spectrum is authorized only above 222 MHz, where there is enough spectrum for a signal to spread without swamping narrowband users. Section 97.313(j) also caps SS at 10 watts PEP.

E1F02.x: A Canadian amateur operating here works under the terms of their Canadian license, capped at US Amateur Extra privileges. They keep their own license's conditions, and the Extra ceiling means the arrangement can never grant more than a US amateur could hold.

E1F03.x: Certification is not required if the amplifier was constructed or modified by an amateur for use at an amateur station. Home-built and amateur-modified gear stays outside the certification regime, which is what keeps homebrewing legal.

E1F04.x: Line A runs roughly parallel to and south of the US border with Canada, from Aberdeen, Washington eastward. It exists to protect Canadian land mobile services, so stations north of it face extra restrictions.

E1F05.x: North of Line A the 420 to 430 MHz segment is off limits, protecting Canadian users of that spectrum. The rest of 70 centimeters, from 430 to 450 MHz, remains available. If you live near the northern border, know this range.

E1F06.x: A Special Temporary Authority grants short-term operation outside the normal rules, and for amateurs the usual basis is experimental communications. An STA is temporary and specific, granted for a stated purpose and period.

E1F07.x: Contacting a business is not itself prohibited. What the rules forbid is communication in which you or your employer holds a pecuniary interest. Ordering a pizza for the club picnic is fine; calling in a parts order for your job is not.

E1F08.x: Section 97.113(a)(2) bars "communications for hire or for material compensation, direct or indirect, paid or promised, except as otherwise provided in these rules." Amateur radio is a noncommercial service, and that principle drives most of §97.113.

E1F09.x: A mesh network is still an amateur station, so every content rule applies to it. Encryption to obscure meaning stays prohibited no matter how modern the transport. Passwords sent in the clear are the price of operating under Part 97.

E1F10.x: Auxiliary stations require a Technician class license or higher. Novice is the one class excluded. Section 97.201(b) also confines auxiliary stations to 2 meters and shorter wavelengths.

E1F11.x: For certification the amplifier must meet the §97.307 spurious emission standards "when operated at the lesser of 1.5 kW PEP or its full output power." Two other conditions ride along: no more than 15 dB gain, and no amplification at all between 26 and 28 MHz.

G0A01.x: RF heats tissue. That thermal effect is the established hazard and the entire basis of the exposure limits. RF is non-ionizing, so it cannot break chemical bonds the way X-rays do; what it can do is deposit enough energy to raise temperature.

G0A02.x: Power at the antenna, antenna gain and pattern, frequency, distance to people and duty cycle all feed the calculation. Every listed factor genuinely matters, so the inclusive answer applies. Exposure is a system property, not a power rating.

G0A03.x: Three routes are acceptable: use the FCC's exemption calculations, run the equations from OET Bulletin 65, or measure with calibrated equipment. All are valid, so the inclusive answer is right. The rule requires an evaluation, not a particular method.

G0A04.x: Time averaging means exposure is assessed over a defined period rather than instant by instant. A transmitter that is idle most of the time delivers less average energy, which is why duty cycle enters the calculation at all.

G0A05.x: Take action to prevent the exposure. The rule requires it: if the evaluation shows fields could exceed the limits in accessible areas, you must fix the situation. Move the antenna, restrict access, reduce power or cut duty cycle.

G0A06.x: If you cannot claim an exemption, you must perform an actual exposure evaluation following OET Bulletin 65. The exemption is the shortcut; failing it does not forbid operating, it obliges you to do the arithmetic.

G0A07.x: Lower duty cycle permits higher power, because the limits are averaged over time. Transmit half as often and you may run twice the power for the same average exposure. That is why SSB and CW are treated more leniently than FM or digital modes.

G0A08.x: Two obligations, and the answer names both: perform the routine evaluation, then keep people out of any area it identifies as over the limit. Doing the evaluation and ignoring the result satisfies nothing.

G0A09.x: A calibrated field strength meter with a calibrated antenna. Both halves matter. An uncalibrated antenna makes the meter's calibration meaningless, since you cannot convert its reading to a field strength you can trust.

G0A10.x: Prevent the antenna from pointing at them while they are there. A beam concentrates its energy in the main lobe, so the exposure problem exists in one direction only. Restricting rotation solves it without touching power or antenna height.

G0A11.x: Confirm that maximum permissible exposure limits are not exceeded where people actually are. An indoor antenna puts the highest field strength in an occupied room, so the evaluation matters far more than it does for a tower-mounted antenna.

G0A12.x: Every station transmitting more than one milliwatt time-averaged. The old blanket exemption for amateurs below certain power levels is gone; the rules now reach essentially all of us, with exemption decided by calculation rather than by license class.

G0B01.x: Only the hot wires. Interrupting them stops the current and leaves the equipment at ground potential. Fusing the neutral or the ground could open the return path while a hot conductor stays live, which is worse than having no protection.

G0B02.x: AWG 12 for a 20-amp breaker. The breaker protects the wire, so the wire must safely carry whatever the breaker allows. Pair the two numbers: 14 gauge with 15 amps, 12 gauge with 20.

G0B03.x: 15 amperes for AWG 14. Same rule as G0B02 asked from the other direction. Fit a 20-amp breaker to 14-gauge wire and the wire becomes the fuse, which is how electrical fires start.

G0B04.x: Outside the building. The point is to divert the surge to earth before it gets indoors. A ground system inside means the strike has already travelled past everything you were trying to protect.

G0B05.x: A GFCI compares current leaving on the hot with current returning on the neutral. Any imbalance means current is finding another path to ground, possibly through a person, so it trips in milliseconds. It protects people, not equipment.

G0B06.x: The electrical safety of your station: wiring, grounding, bonding and overcurrent protection. The NEC is adopted into law by most localities, so it governs your shack even though the FCC has nothing to say about wiring.

G0B07.x: Check both the weight rating and the service life. Harness webbing degrades from ultraviolet light and age even when it looks fine, so a harness found in the garage may be well past its date. Inspect before every climb.

G0B08.x: Lock out and tag every circuit feeding the tower. Rotators, lights and amplifiers can be energized remotely by someone who has no idea you are up there. Locking the breaker and tagging it is what guarantees they cannot.

G0B09.x: Run it in a well-ventilated area. Engine exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which is colourless, odourless and kills without warning. Generators must never run in a garage or basement, even with a door open.

G0B10.x: Lead transfers to your hands and then to whatever you eat. Wash before eating, and do not eat at the bench. The solder fumes are mostly flux rather than lead, since lead does not vaporize much at soldering temperatures.

G0B11.x: All ground rods must be bonded together with every other ground at the site. Separate grounds sit at different potentials during a surge, and the difference drives current through your equipment as it equalizes. One bonded system, not several.

G0B12.x: An interlock removes dangerous voltages when the cabinet is opened, usually by cutting the high-voltage supply as the cover comes off. It protects whoever opens the equipment from a supply they forgot was live. Never defeat one to work on a running amplifier.

G0B13.x: Where the feed lines enter the building, on a grounded panel. Catching the surge at the entry point keeps it out of the shack. An arrestor further inside has already let the energy reach your equipment.

G1A01.x: Four HF bands hold Extra-only segments at the bottom end: 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters. A General may not transmit there. Learn those four together, because G1A08 asks the same thing from the Extra side.

G1A02.x: Thirty meters is CW and data only, for everyone. No phone, no image, no exceptions by license class. It is also a narrow band shared with other services, which is why the FCC keeps voice off it entirely.

G1A03.x: Same band, same reason as G1A02. Thirty meters allows only CW and data emissions, so image transmission is out along with phone. If a question about 30 meters offers a mode other than CW or data, that mode is prohibited.

G1A05.x: On 40 meters the General phone privileges begin at 7.175 MHz. Everything from 7.125 to 7.175 is reserved for Extra. Remember 7.175 as your lower edge on 40 meter voice.

G1A06.x: Secondary status cuts both ways. You must not cause harmful interference to the primary service, and you have to accept whatever interference it sends your way. You still get to operate there. You just have no standing to complain.

G1A07.x: CW is authorized "on any frequency authorized to the control operator," and a General holds the whole 10-meter band, 28.0 to 29.7 MHz. So CW is legal across all of it. That §97.305(a) principle answers a lot of CW questions.

G1A08.x: The bands with Extra-exclusive segments are 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters. Same four as G1A01, viewed from the other direction. No exclusive Extra spectrum exists on 30, 17, 12 or 10 meters.

G1A09.x: General phone on 15 meters runs 21.275 to 21.450 MHz, so 21300 kHz sits comfortably inside. Watch the units when a question mixes kHz and MHz: 21300 kHz is 21.300 MHz.

G1A10.x: Section 97.205(b) excludes 28.0 to 29.5 MHz from repeater use, which leaves the top of the band. Repeaters on 10 meters live above 29.5 MHz, and 29.6 MHz is the common simplex-repeater output.

G1A11.x: Where a General does not get the whole voice segment, the missing piece is always at the bottom, reserved for Extra. Generals work the upper portion. That pattern holds on every band, so the answer is the upper part of the segment.

G1B01.x: Structures over 200 feet above ground require FAA notification and FCC registration, and so do shorter ones near a public use airport. Two hundred feet is the number, and note it is measured above ground level at the site, not above sea level.

G1B02.x: A beacon "must not concurrently transmit on more than 1 channel in the same amateur service frequency band, from the same station location." One beacon per band per site. Nothing stops you running beacons on several different bands.

G1B03.x: The definition gives the purpose directly: a beacon transmits "for the purposes of observation of propagation and reception or other related experimental activities." Propagation observation is the phrase to match.

G1B04.x: You generally may not retransmit non-amateur signals, but §97.113(c) carves out propagation and weather forecast information originating from US Government stations. It must be occasional rather than routine, which the rule states plainly.

G1B05.x: Section 97.111(b) lists the permitted one-way transmissions, and paragraph (5) covers "transmissions necessary to assisting persons learning, or improving proficiency in, the international Morse code." Code practice made the list; general broadcasting never does.

G1B06.x: This is the PRB-1 standard, written into §97.15(b). Local regulation of amateur antenna structures "must have a reasonable and clearly defined objective" and constitute the minimum practical regulation, and it must reasonably accommodate amateur communications. Reasonable accommodation and minimum practical are the two phrases.

G1B07.x: Q signals, prosigns and the usual on-air shorthand are fine. What the rule forbids is "messages encoded for the purpose of obscuring their meaning." Standard abbreviations aid communication rather than hide it, so intent is the dividing line.

G1B08.x: You may work amateurs anywhere except in countries whose administrations have notified the ITU that they object. The objection must be filed with the ITU. Same rule tested in T1D01 on the Technician exam.

G1B09.x: On HF the only segment where a beacon may run under automatic control is 28.20 to 28.30 MHz. Ten meters again, and the same range the Technician exam asks about.

G1B10.x: Section 97.203(c) is one line: beacon transmitter power "must not exceed 100 W." A beacon exists to report whether a path is open, and more power would only distort that picture.

G1B11.x: Where Part 97 is silent, stations must operate "in accordance with good engineering and good amateur practice," and the FCC decides what that means. Not the ARRL, not your club, not the frequency coordinator. The Commission is the arbiter.

G1C01.x: 10.140 MHz sits in the 30-meter band, 10.100 to 10.150 MHz, and §97.313(c)(1) caps that whole segment at 200 watts PEP for everyone. Thirty meters is the low-power band, so the answer is 200 watts.

G1C02.x: Twelve meters carries no special restriction, so the general ceiling applies: 1.5 kW PEP, or 1500 watts. Only a short list of segments deviates from that, and 30 meters is the one most likely to appear on your exam.

G1C03.x: The rule requires that on all 60-meter spectrum, "amateur operators shall ensure that their emissions do not occupy more than 2.8 kHz." That figure matches a normal SSB signal, which is why standard voice gear works there unmodified.

G1C04.x: Sixty-meter power is specified as ERP referenced to a dipole, so the FCC needs to know your antenna gain to police it. If you use anything other than a dipole, keep the manufacturer's gain data or your own calculations in your station records.

G1C05.x: A General on 10 meters gets the full 1500 watts PEP. The 200-watt cap that applies to Technicians on 28.0 to 28.5 MHz is tied to the operator class, not the band, so it does not follow you after you upgrade.

G1C06.x: The 1.8 MHz band is 160 meters, and it carries no special power restriction. The general limit applies: 1500 watts PEP. When a power question names a band with no listed exception, 1500 watts is the default.

G1C07.x: An amateur station may use any digital technique "whose technical characteristics have been documented publicly." Public documentation is what keeps a mode from counting as an obscuring code. No FCC approval or certification is needed, only publication.

G1C11.x: All amateur power limits are written as PEP output measured at the transmitter, not input power and not what the amplifier draws from the wall. Section 97.3 defines PEP as the average power supplied to the antenna transmission line at the crest of the modulation envelope.

G1D01.x: Element credit for an expired license survives indefinitely, as long as the license was General, Advanced or Extra and was not revoked. You show proof of the old grant and the VEs give credit for the written element it represented. Revocation is the one thing that kills it.

G1D02.x: A VE may administer exams one full class below their own license. General class VEs administer Technician exams only. Extra or Advanced is needed for General exams, and Extra alone for Extra exams.

G1D03.x: An unexpired CSCE gives you the new privileges immediately, before the FCC database catches up. With a General CSCE in hand a Technician may work any General or Technician segment. Identify with the AG indicator while doing it, per §97.119(f)(2).

G1D04.x: Every amateur exam session takes a team of at least three accredited VEs, and for a Technician exam each must hold General or higher. Three is the number, and all three observe the entire examination.

G1D05.x: The station is a US station, so US rules follow it regardless of where the operator is sitting. Section 97.7 requires a control operator holding an FCC operator/primary station license. Your physical location does not change what the station needs.

G1D06.x: The AG indicator is required whenever you use the General privileges you have not yet been granted on paper. Operating inside Technician limits needs no indicator. Once the upgrade appears in the FCC database, you stop using AG entirely.

G1D07.x: Volunteer Examiners are accredited by a Volunteer Examiner Coordinator, the VEC. The FCC certifies VECs and the VECs accredit individual VEs. The Commission never accredits a VE directly.

G1D08.x: Citizenship is not a requirement anywhere in §97.509. What matters is holding an FCC-granted license of General class or above, being at least 18, and never having had a license revoked or suspended.

G1D09.x: A CSCE is good for 365 days of element credit. One year, and then the credit is gone and the element must be passed again. Note that it gives operating privileges too, under §97.9(b), until the upgrade posts.

G1D10.x: A VE must be at least 18 years of age. There is no upper age limit and no minimum time licensed, just 18 and the required license class.

G1D11.x: Once the two-year grace period lapses the license is gone, but the element credit is not. Show proof of the expired General grant and you keep Element 3 credit. You still have to sit the current Element 2 exam, because that credit does not carry.

G1D12.x: A remotely controlled station is operating where the transmitter is, not where you are. Point the radio at South America and that country's regulations govern the transmission. Your US license does not extend its rules abroad.

G1E01.x: A third party is disqualified if they were previously licensed and that license was revoked or suspended and not reinstated. Ordinary unlicensed people are welcome to speak. The bar is aimed at someone the FCC has already sanctioned.

G1E02.x: The repeater's control operator sets what the repeater may transmit, and 10-meter privileges require General or higher. A Technician may feed the input on 2 meters, but the General class control operator is what makes the 10-meter output legal.

G1E03.x: Outside the automatic control segments, an automatically controlled digital station may only respond. Section 97.221(c) requires that it be "responding to interrogation by a station under local or remote control," and that its transmissions stay within 500 Hz.

G1E04.x: Three separate rules each impose a duty to avoid interference: proximity to an FCC monitoring station, operating on a secondary allocation, and running spread spectrum. Since every listed condition carries that obligation, the inclusive answer is correct.

G1E05.x: Even with a third-party agreement in place, the content limits of §97.117 still apply: matters incidental to amateur radio and remarks of a personal character, plus emergency and disaster relief traffic. An agreement opens the door, it does not remove the content rules.

G1E06.x: The ITU divides the world into three regions. Region 1 is Europe, Africa and northern Asia, Region 3 is the rest of Asia and Oceania, and Region 2 is the Americas. North and South America are Region 2.

G1E07.x: Section 97.111 lists who an amateur station may communicate with, and unlicensed Part 15 devices are not on that list. Sharing spectrum with Wi-Fi in the 2.4 GHz band does not create permission to work those stations. No part of the band.

G1E08.x: Spread spectrum is capped hard: "No station may transmit with a transmitter output exceeding 10 W PEP when the station is transmitting a SS emission type." Ten watts, because SS energy spreads across spectrum other users occupy.

G1E10.x: Those five frequencies carry the International Beacon Project network, where synchronized beacons around the world transmit in rotation so operators can gauge propagation. Transmitting there breaks a shared resource, which §97.101(a) treats as poor amateur practice.

G1E11.x: Automatic control for digital stations is wide open on 6 meters and everything shorter. On HF it is confined to narrow slices such as 28.120 to 28.189 MHz and 21.090 to 21.100 MHz. Above 50 MHz anywhere, below it only in listed segments.

G1E12.x: Section 97.115 sets conditions on third-party traffic but says nothing about how the station is controlled. Remote control neither adds restrictions nor removes them. If the message would be legal at the radio, it is legal from a distance.

G2A01.src: ARRL band plans; ARRL Operating Manual
G2A01.x: One convention covers all the sideband questions: 20 meters and up is upper sideband, 40 meters and down is lower. At 14 MHz and above you use USB. Learn the dividing line once and G2A01 through G2A04 all fall out of it.

G2A02.x: The three lowest phone bands use lower sideband: 160, 75 and 40 meters. Everything from 20 meters upward uses upper. The break sits between 40 and 20, with no phone on 30 meters in between.

G2A03.x: SSB above 50 MHz is upper sideband, following the same rule as 20 meters and up. VHF and UHF weak-signal work is also horizontally polarized by convention, which is worth remembering alongside it.

G2A04.x: Seventeen and 12 meters are both above 14 MHz, so both use upper sideband. Any band higher in frequency than 20 meters follows the USB convention.

G2A05.x: Single sideband dominates HF voice. It fits roughly 3 kHz where AM needs 6, and it puts all the transmitter's power into the one sideband that carries the intelligence rather than into a carrier that carries none.

G2A06.x: Two advantages at once, and the answer names both: half the bandwidth of AM and far better power efficiency, since nothing is wasted on a carrier or a redundant second sideband. That combination is why SSB displaced AM on HF.

G2A07.x: SSB starts as double-sideband AM, then the carrier and one sideband are suppressed. Both sidebands carry identical information, so discarding one loses nothing while halving the bandwidth.

G2A08.x: Say your call sign once, during a pause between transmissions. Not "break," not "contact," and not repeatedly. Your call sign identifies you and requests entry in one step, which is why it is the accepted practice.

G2A09.x: There is no rule requiring it and no technical reason for it. The LSB convention on the low bands is simply what equipment manufacturers and operators settled on decades ago. Custom, not regulation.

G2A10.x: VOX keys the transmitter from your voice, so your hands stay free. The tradeoff is that room noise can trip it and pauses can drop you mid-sentence, which is why many operators still prefer a foot switch.

G2A11.x: CQ DX means the caller wants contacts outside their own country. From the contiguous 48 states that means stations outside the lower 48, so Alaska and Hawaii count. If you are inside the 48 and hear it, the call is not for you.

G2A12.x: ALC responds to how hard your audio drives the transmitter, so microphone or transmit audio gain is the control that sets it. Adjust until ALC just registers on peaks. Beyond that you are only adding distortion and splatter.

G2B01.x: Part 97 settles it: "no frequency will be assigned for the exclusive use of any station." Nobody owns a frequency, not nets, not repeater groups, not contesters. The one exception in §97.101(c) is emergency traffic, which gets priority.

G2B02.x: Acknowledge them and find out what they need. Distress traffic outranks whatever you were doing, and §97.403 lets you use any means at your disposal to help. Do not simply move aside and hope somebody else takes it.

G2B03.x: Work it out with the other stations in a way everyone can accept. Propagation shifts constantly and nobody involved did anything wrong. Since no station holds a frequency exclusively, cooperation is the only mechanism available.

G2B04.x: Leave 150 to 500 Hz between CW signals. A CW signal is only about 150 Hz wide, so that spacing keeps you clear of the other operator's receive filter without wasting band space.

G2B05.x: Two to 3 kHz for SSB, because the signal itself occupies about 3 kHz. Space them closer and your sidebands land inside the neighbouring station's passband. Compare with the 150 to 500 Hz needed for far narrower CW.

G2B06.src: ITU-R Rec. M.1172; ARRL Operating Manual
G2B06.x: Ask before you call. Send "QRL?" with your call sign on CW, or ask whether the frequency is in use on phone. A frequency can sound clear when one end of an existing contact is simply out of your propagation path.

G2B07.x: Follow the voluntary band plan. It is not FCC-enforced, but it keeps CW, digital, SSB and beacons out of each other's way, and ignoring it counts against good amateur practice under §97.101(a).

G2B08.x: That segment is the 6-meter DX window. Stations inside the 48 contiguous states use it only for contacts with stations outside the 48, keeping it clear for the rare openings that make long-haul 6-meter work possible.

G2B09.x: Only a licensed amateur. RACES runs on amateur frequencies under Part 97, so the control operator needs an FCC amateur license plus certification by the civil defense organization. An emergency does not waive the license requirement.

G2B10.x: Agree on a backup frequency in advance. Nets get stepped on and propagation fails, and negotiating a new frequency while the net is falling apart does not work. Announce the alternate before you need it.

G2B11.x: One hour per week. The rule permits RACES drills and tests "not to exceed a total time of 1 hour per week" without special authorization. More than that requires approval from the state emergency planning officer.

G2C01.x: QSK means your receiver is live between the elements of your own characters, so you hear another station the instant they start sending. It makes CW feel like a conversation rather than an exchange of speeches, since anyone can break in mid-word.

G2C02.x: QRS means send more slowly. Its opposite is QRQ, send faster. If someone sends QRS they are struggling to copy you, so slow down rather than repeating at the same speed.

G2C03.x: KN closes the transmission to everyone except the station you are working. Plain K invites anyone to call; adding the N narrows it. Use KN when you are in a contact and do not want new callers joining.

G2C04.x: QRL? asks whether the frequency is in use, literally "are you busy?" Send it before calling CQ on a frequency that sounds clear. A bare QRL as a statement means the frequency is busy.

G2C05.x: Answer at a speed you can copy comfortably, and never faster than the CQ was sent. Replying faster than someone can receive gets you nowhere, and matching their speed signals that the contact will work.

G2C06.x: Zero beat means tuning your transmit frequency onto the other station's, so the audio tone difference between you drops toward zero. Being exactly on frequency puts you in the middle of their filter, where you are loudest.

G2C07.x: A trailing C reports a chirpy signal, meaning the frequency shifts slightly each time the key closes. It usually points at a power supply sagging under keying load. The RST report also uses X for a steady signal and K for key clicks.

G2C08.src: ARRL Operating Manual; ITU-R Rec. M.1677
G2C08.x: AR, sent as one run-together character, marks the end of a formal message. Do not confuse it with SK, which ends the entire contact, or with K, which simply invites a reply.

G2C09.x: QSL means I have received and understood. As a question it asks whether you were copied. The paper QSL card takes its name from this signal, since the card is written confirmation of the same thing.

G2C10.x: QRN is natural static, the crash of distant lightning. Keep it apart from QRM, which is interference from other stations. QRN is nature, QRM is people.

G2C11.x: QRV means I am ready. It reports that you are standing by and able to receive, which is why net operators use it to check in.

G2D01.src: ARRL Volunteer Monitor Program; FCC agreement
G2D01.x: The Volunteer Monitor Program is licensed amateurs formally enlisted, under an agreement between the ARRL and the FCC, to monitor the bands for rules violations. It replaced the older Official Observer program in 2019.

G2D02.x: The aim is self-regulation: encourage amateurs to comply voluntarily and document the cases that genuinely need FCC attention. Monitors have no enforcement power of their own. They gather evidence and educate.

G2D03.x: Several monitors take beam headings on the repeater input from their own locations and compare them. Where the bearings intersect is the transmitter. One bearing gives a line, and it takes two or more to fix a position.

G2D04.src: Map projection theory; ARRL Antenna Book
G2D04.x: An azimuthal projection centred on your station shows true bearings and distances from that one point. Straight lines out from the centre are great-circle paths, so you read the beam heading to anywhere directly off the map.

G2D05.x: Repeat CQ a few times, say "this is," give your call sign a few times, then stop and listen. The rhythm matters more than the words: calling too long means transmitting over the people trying to answer you.

G2D06.x: Long path is 180 degrees from the short-path heading, going the other way around the Earth. It is a longer route so it needs better conditions, but sometimes the long way is open when the direct path is not.

G2D07.x: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta opens the standard phonetic alphabet, used internationally by aviation, the military and amateur radio alike. Sticking to the standard words matters because improvised substitutes are exactly what gets misheard.

G2D08.x: Logs are no longer required by the FCC, but they help you answer if the Commission asks about your station's operation. They also serve awards and QSL work, which is why most operators keep one anyway.

G2D09.x: Nothing special. Contest rules do not change FCC requirements, so you still identify at least every 10 minutes and at the end of each contact. Contest exchanges are brief, but the identification rule is unchanged.

G2D10.src: ITU-R Rec. M.1172; ARRL Operating Manual
G2D10.x: QRP means low power, conventionally 5 watts output or less on CW and 10 watts on phone. It comes from the Q signal QRP, which means reduce power.

G2D11.x: An early signal report tells each operator what the path will support, so you can decide whether to slow down, repeat more, or switch modes. It is practical information at the start of a contact rather than a courtesy.

G2E01.x: RTTY sent as AFSK through an SSB transmitter uses lower sideband, which puts the mark and space tones in the same relationship as a direct FSK transmitter. Note this is the exception: the newer WSJT modes use USB instead.

G2E02.x: VARA is a high-throughput digital protocol used with Winlink, adapting its speed to conditions on the path. It moves email and files considerably faster than the older PACTOR modes it competes with.

G2E03.x: Interference on an ARQ link shows up as repeated retries, slower throughput, and eventually a dropped connection. All the listed symptoms are genuine, so the inclusive answer applies. The protocol is protecting your data by resending it.

G2E04.x: FT8 alternates 15-second slots, so answer in the slot the caller is not using and pick a clear audio frequency. Transmitting in their slot means neither of you hears the other.

G2E05.x: JT65, JT9, FT4 and FT8 all use upper sideband. This is where the WSJT family departs from RTTY, which uses LSB. If you set the wrong sideband nothing decodes, since the tones land inverted.

G2E06.x: A 170 Hz shift between mark and space is the amateur HF standard, paired with 45 baud. Commercial and military RTTY used wider shifts; amateurs settled on 170 Hz to keep the signal narrow.

G2E07.x: Your computer clock must be right to within about a second. FT8 slices time into fixed 15-second windows and decodes on that schedule, so a clock off by a few seconds means the software looks for signals in the wrong interval.

G2E08.x: Digital modes on 20 meters cluster between 14.070 and 14.100 MHz. That 30 kHz window holds RTTY, PSK and the WSJT modes, which is why FT8 at 14.074 sits inside it.

G2E09.x: You cannot join. PACTOR is a point-to-point ARQ link between exactly two stations, with each end acknowledging the other's blocks. There is no provision for a third participant, unlike a plain conversational mode.

G2E10.x: Send a connect message on the gateway's published frequency. Gateways advertise their frequencies and operating hours, and your software then negotiates the link automatically.

G2E11.x: AREDN builds a high-speed data network from repurposed Wi-Fi hardware, carrying services that ordinary HF data rates cannot: video, file transfer, voice over IP. It is designed for emergencies and community events where normal infrastructure is unavailable.

G2E12.x: Winlink is all of these: a radio email system, a network of gateway stations, and a service usable over both HF and VHF. Since every listed description is accurate, the inclusive answer is right.

G2E13.x: A Remote Message Server is a gateway, the station bridging radio and the internet so your message reaches ordinary email. Same idea as an IRLP node bridging repeaters.

G2E14.x: An FSK signal that looks tuned but will not decode usually means inverted mark and space, the wrong baud rate or shift, or the wrong sideband. All the listed faults produce exactly this symptom, so the inclusive answer applies.

G2E15.src: WSJT-X documentation; ARRL 20 m band plan
G2E15.x: FT8 on 20 meters lives around 14.074 to 14.077 MHz, inside the wider digital segment that starts at 14.070. It is the busiest few kilohertz in amateur radio most days.

G3A01.src: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center; ITU-R Rec. P.533
G3A01.x: More sunspots means more solar ultraviolet, which ionizes the F region more heavily. A denser F region bends higher frequencies back to Earth, so 15, 12 and 10 meters come alive. High sunspot numbers open the high bands.

G3A02.x: A sudden ionospheric disturbance floods the D region with ionization, and the D region absorbs rather than refracts. Absorption falls as frequency rises, so the low bands go out first while the higher frequencies survive longer.

G3A03.x: Ultraviolet and X-rays travel at the speed of light, and the Sun is about 93 million miles away, so they arrive in roughly 8 minutes. Keep it apart from a coronal mass ejection, which is matter rather than light and takes far longer.

G3A04.x: At solar minimum the F region never ionizes enough to return the highest bands, so 15, 12 and 10 meters are the first to close and the least dependable. They are also the bands that reward solar maximum most.

G3A05.x: Solar flux index is the Sun's radio noise measured at a wavelength of 10.7 centimeters, about 2800 MHz. It tracks solar activity more directly than counting sunspots, and it updates daily rather than being smoothed over a month.

G3A06.x: A geomagnetic storm is a temporary disturbance of Earth's magnetic field, usually triggered by charged particles arriving from the Sun. It is a magnetic event rather than an ionizing one, which is why its effects differ from a flare's.

G3A07.x: Twenty meters works worldwide in daylight at any point in the solar cycle. It sits low enough that even a weakly ionized F region returns it, and high enough to escape most D region absorption. That balance is why it is the reliable DX band.

G3A08.x: Geomagnetic storms hit high latitudes hardest, because Earth's field funnels the incoming particles toward the poles. Paths crossing auroral regions degrade or disappear while equatorial paths often stay usable.

G3A09.x: The same activity that wrecks HF at high latitudes creates auroras, and auroral curtains reflect VHF signals. Six meters and 2 meters open to contacts that would otherwise be impossible, though the signals come back distorted and raspy.

G3A10.x: The Sun rotates about once every 27 days as seen from Earth, so an active region faces us, turns away, and comes back around. Conditions repeat on that rhythm because you are seeing the same region again.

G3A11.x: A coronal mass ejection is a cloud of matter, not light, so it crawls compared with a flare's radiation: 15 hours to several days. The flare arrives in 8 minutes, the CME days later, which is why the two effects are separated in time.

G3A12.x: The K-index reports short-term geomagnetic stability, measured over three-hour intervals on a 0 to 9 scale. Low is quiet and above about 4 means a storm. Pair it with the A-index, which is the longer-term view.

G3A13.x: The A-index is the long-term measure, a daily figure derived from the day's K readings. K tells you what the field is doing now; A tells you what it has been doing. Short-term is K, long-term is A.

G3A14.x: Coronal holes emit fast solar wind streams, and the charged particles they send disturb Earth's magnetic field. The result on HF is much like a geomagnetic storm: degraded paths, worst at high latitudes.

G3B01.x: The same signal reaching you both the short way and the long way around the Earth travels very different distances, so the long-path copy arrives measurably later. You hear it as a faint echo just behind the direct signal.

G3B02.x: MUF depends on the path, the time of day, the season and the current state of solar activity. Every listed factor genuinely moves it, so the inclusive answer applies. That is also why MUF is predicted rather than simply looked up.

G3B03.x: Work just below the MUF. The higher the frequency, the less D region absorption you suffer, so the least attenuated path is the highest one the ionosphere will still bend back. Go above the MUF and the signal leaves for space.

G3B04.x: Automated receiver networks such as the Reverse Beacon Network and PSK Reporter log who is hearing whom and post it on the web. Transmit briefly, then look up where you were decoded. It is real measurement of your own signal rather than a prediction.

G3B05.x: Between the LUF and the MUF is the usable window: the ionosphere refracts those signals back to Earth. Above the MUF they punch through into space; below the LUF the D region absorbs them before they get anywhere.

G3B06.x: Below the lowest usable frequency the signal is absorbed before it reaches the far end. The energy does not go to space, it goes into heat in the D region. Absorption rises as frequency falls, which is what sets the LUF.

G3B07.x: Lowest Usable Frequency, and the definition is specific to one path between two points. Below it, absorption kills the signal. LUF is the floor, MUF the ceiling, and both are path-dependent.

G3B08.x: Maximum Usable Frequency for a given path between two points. Above it the ionosphere no longer bends the wave enough to return it. Since it depends on the path, two stations can have very different MUFs at the same moment.

G3B09.src: ITU-R Rec. P.533; ARRL Antenna Book
G3B09.x: About 2,500 miles per hop off the F2 region, which sits roughly 200 to 400 km up. The higher the reflecting layer, the longer the geometry allows each hop to reach.

G3B10.src: ITU-R Rec. P.533; ARRL Antenna Book
G3B10.x: About 1,200 miles per E region hop, from a layer near 110 km. Half the F2 distance because the layer is roughly a third the height. Learn the pair together: E gives 1,200, F2 gives 2,500.

G3B11.x: If the LUF climbs above the MUF the usable window closes entirely and no ordinary skywave path exists. The floor has risen above the ceiling, so every frequency is either absorbed or lost to space.

G3B12.x: Summer means thunderstorms, and lightning is a broadband noise source that propagates efficiently on the low bands. Eighty and 160 meters can be buried in static in July while staying quiet and workable in January.

G3C01.x: The D region is lowest, roughly 50 to 90 km up. Going outward the order is D, E, then F. Being deepest in the atmosphere is exactly why it absorbs instead of refracting: collisions there are frequent.

G3C02.x: At a given angle of incidence, the critical frequency is the highest one still refracted back to Earth. Above it the wave escapes. It is the physical basis for the MUF, which applies the same idea to a specific path.

G3C03.x: F2 is the highest region, so the geometry of a bounce off it covers more ground. Higher reflection point means a shallower angle can still come back down, and that stretches each hop to about 2,500 miles.

G3C04.x: Critical angle is the highest takeoff angle that still returns a wave to Earth for the conditions of the moment. Steeper than that and the signal goes through the layer rather than being bent back. It moves with ionization, so it is not a fixed number.

G3C05.x: Sunlight creates the D region, and the D region absorbs the low bands. That is why 160 through 40 meters shrink to local coverage by day and open up for long distance after dark, once the D region has recombined away.

G3C06.x: Scatter signals flutter. The energy arrives from many small scattering points that move and change, so the sum rises and falls rapidly. Weak and fluttery together is the signature.

G3C07.x: Scattered energy takes many paths of slightly different length, so copies arrive spread out in time and out of phase. That smearing is heard as distortion, the same mechanism as multipath on VHF but with far more paths involved.

G3C08.x: Scattering redirects only a small fraction of your signal into the skip zone. Most of the energy continues on its intended path, so what fills the gap is the leftovers. Weak is expected.

G3C09.x: Scatter is what fills the skip zone, the dead ring that is too far for ground wave and too near for the first hop. Irregularities in the ionosphere and terrain deflect a little energy down into it.

G3C10.x: NVIS fires almost straight up on MF or HF and lets the ionosphere drop the signal back over a radius of a few hundred miles. It fills the skip zone deliberately, which is why emergency communicators use it for regional coverage.

G3C11.x: The D region absorbs most strongly below 10 MHz during daylight. It exists only while the Sun is up, and its effect falls off as frequency rises, which is why the low bands suffer and 20 meters does not.

G4A01.x: A notch filter puts a deep, very narrow null at one frequency, which is exactly the shape needed to kill a steady carrier sitting inside your passband. It removes the heterodyne while leaving the voice around it intact.

G4A02.x: Switching sidebands flips your receiver's passband to the other side of the carrier. An interfering signal that fell inside the filter may now fall outside it. The CW note you want stays the same pitch, so nothing is lost by trying.

G4A03.x: A noise blanker watches for the sharp leading edge of an impulse and drops receiver gain for the microseconds it lasts. Ignition noise and power line arcing are pulses, so blanking them costs almost no audio. It does nothing for steady hiss.

G4A04.x: Tuning the plate circuit through resonance produces a pronounced dip in plate current. The dip is the indicator you tune for, because at resonance the tube's load looks resistive and it draws least current.

G4A05.x: ALC feeds a control voltage back to the exciter so the amplifier cannot be driven past its linear range. Without it, cranking up the transceiver simply produces distortion and splatter rather than more clean output.

G4A06.src: Impedance matching theory; ARRL Antenna Book
G4A06.x: A tuner presents the transmitter the load it wants to see, so it delivers full power into the feed line instead of folding back. Note what it does not do: nothing changes at the antenna, so feed line SWR beyond the tuner is unaffected.

G4A07.x: Noise reduction guesses which parts of the audio are signal and which are noise, and the aggressive settings guess wrong. Push it too far and voices go hollow and watery. Use the least amount that makes copy comfortable.

G4A08.x: Adjust LOAD for the output you want while keeping plate current within the tube's rating. TUNE finds resonance, LOAD sets how hard the tube works. The two interact, so you go back and forth between them.

G4A09.x: The amplifier's relays need a few milliseconds to move the antenna from the transceiver to the amplifier output. Sending RF before they settle arcs the contacts and can destroy them. The delay simply lets the mechanics finish first.

G4A10.x: A keyer turns paddle closures into correctly timed dots and dashes at a set speed. You still form the characters; the keyer handles the element lengths and spacing so your fist stays even.

G4A11.x: ALC is designed for the varying envelope of speech. AFSK data has constant amplitude, so any ALC action modulates it and smears the signal. Set drive so ALC never activates, then leave the level alone.

G4A12.x: Two VFOs let you transmit on one frequency and listen on another, which is split operation. DX stations use it to keep their transmit frequency clear of the pileup calling them.

G4A13.x: An attenuator cuts everything ahead of the first mixer, keeping a very strong signal from overloading the front end. You lose sensitivity you did not need, and in exchange the distortion products that were burying weaker signals disappear.

G4B01.x: Horizontal and vertical channel amplifiers belong to an oscilloscope. The vertical channel carries the signal you are looking at, the horizontal drives the time base that sweeps it across the screen.

G4B02.x: A voltmeter reduces a signal to a single number. A scope shows the waveform against time, so you can see shape, distortion, ringing and timing. For anything more complex than a steady level, the picture is the point.

G4B03.x: Keying waveform is about shape over time: how fast the envelope rises and falls. Only a scope shows that. Rise times that are too abrupt generate key clicks, and you cannot see the problem on a meter.

G4B04.x: Feed the vertical input from an attenuated sample of the transmitter's RF output. Attenuated matters. Full transmitter output into a scope input will destroy it, so the sample comes through a suitable pad or coupler.

G4B05.x: A voltmeter in parallel with the circuit draws some current of its own, which changes the very voltage you are measuring. High input impedance keeps that current negligible, so the reading reflects the circuit rather than the meter.

G4B06.x: A digital meter resolves more digits and removes the guesswork of reading a needle against a scale. Note the flip side, tested in G4B09: for peaking or nulling an adjustment, a moving needle beats a jittering number.

G4B07.x: Two audio tones that are not harmonically related. Non-harmonic matters, because any intermodulation products the amplifier creates then land on frequencies no legitimate harmonic could occupy, which makes them unmistakable.

G4B08.x: A two-tone test measures linearity. A perfectly linear amplifier reproduces both tones and nothing else; a nonlinear one manufactures intermodulation products between them. Those extra products are the measurement.

G4B09.x: When you are peaking or nulling something, a needle shows the direction and rate of change at a glance. A digital display flickers through unrelated digits and you lose the trend. Analog wins for adjusting, digital for reading.

G4B10.x: A directional wattmeter reads forward and reflected power separately, and SWR follows from their ratio. Many meters compute it for you and show it directly on the scale.

G4B11.x: The analyzer needs to see the whole system it is measuring, so connect the antenna with its feed line. What you get is the SWR at the shack end, which is what your transmitter actually sees.

G4B12.x: An analyzer measures its own weak test signal, so a strong nearby transmitter arriving on the same antenna swamps that measurement and the readings go wrong. If a neighbouring station is active, wait rather than trusting the numbers.

G4B13.src: ARRL Antenna Book; transmission line theory
G4B13.x: An antenna analyzer measures complex impedance, so it can characterize a length of coax as well as an antenna: its impedance, electrical length and velocity factor. Useful for finding a cable's actual quarter-wave frequency.

G4C01.x: A bypass capacitor gives RF a low-impedance path to ground before it reaches the audio stages, while leaving the audio frequencies untouched. It works because reactance falls as frequency rises, so the capacitor is nearly a short at RF.

G4C02.x: An arc is a broadband noise generator. Each spark is a fast pulse, and fast pulses contain energy across an enormous span of frequencies. That is why arcing shows up as a buzz right across the bands rather than on one frequency.

G4C03.x: Distorted, unintelligible speech. RF from an SSB transmitter gets rectified in an audio stage that was never meant to demodulate anything, so the result is a rough approximation of your voice rather than a clean copy.

G4C04.x: On-and-off humming or clicking, following your keying. CW is a carrier switched on and off, so the interference switches with it. The rhythm of the sound matches your fist, which makes the source easy to identify.

G4C05.x: A ground wire is only a ground at DC. At RF its inductance can make it look like a high impedance, or even resonate, so the chassis it was supposed to hold at zero volts floats at high RF potential instead. Touch it and you get burned.

G4C06.x: A ground conductor about a quarter wavelength long behaves as a resonant element rather than a short, presenting high impedance at its far end. The result is high RF voltage on equipment enclosures, which is the same mechanism as G4C05.

G4C07.x: A lightning strike carries enough current to melt solder, so a soldered joint can simply vanish at the moment you most need it intact. Lightning grounds use mechanical connections: clamps, exothermic welds, crimps.

G4C08.x: A ferrite choke adds impedance to common-mode current, the component flowing the same direction on every conductor in the cable. The signal you want is differential and passes unaffected, so the choke removes interference without touching the audio.

G4C09.x: Bond the enclosures together so there is no potential difference to drive current between them. A ground loop exists because two grounded points sit at slightly different voltages; bonding removes the difference rather than the loop.

G4C10.x: Hum reports. A ground loop lets AC line current circulate through your audio grounds, and that current appears as 60 Hz hum riding on your modulation. Everyone hears it except you.

G4C11.x: Bond every enclosure together. Hot spots appear where two pieces of equipment sit at different RF potentials, so tying them to a common bonded system removes the difference that makes a spot hot.

G4C12.x: Grounding the chassis means a fault inside the equipment goes to ground and trips the breaker instead of leaving the case live. Without it, an insulation failure can put line voltage on the metal you are touching.

G4D01.x: A speech processor raises the average level of your voice relative to its peaks, so the signal sounds louder without exceeding the same peak limit. It buys apparent loudness rather than more peak power.

G4D02.x: Average power goes up while peak envelope power stays where it was. Speech is mostly quiet punctuated by peaks, so compressing that range puts more energy on the air within the same PEP limit. That is why processing helps readability.

G4D03.x: Overdone processing brings distortion, splatter into adjacent frequencies, and a harsh unnatural sound, and it can pump up background noise along with your voice. All the listed effects are real, so the inclusive answer applies.

G4D04.x: An S meter reads received signal strength. It says nothing about your transmitter, and its calibration varies between radios, which is why reports from different stations are not directly comparable.

G4D05.x: Twenty dB is a factor of 100 in power, since 10 to the power of 20 over 10 is 100. So 20 dB over S9 is a hundred times the power of S9. The two dB rules cover it: 10 dB is ten times, and 20 dB is ten times ten.

G4D06.x: One S unit is 6 dB by the standard, which is a factor of about four in power. Real receivers rarely match that exactly below S9, but 6 dB is the figure the exam wants and the basis for G4D07.

G4D07.x: One S unit is 6 dB, and 6 dB in power is 10 to the power of 0.6, which is 3.98. So roughly four times the power to move S8 to S9. Quadrupling your output to gain one S unit is why chasing S units with power rarely pays.

G4D08.x: Lower sideband puts your energy below the displayed carrier, so a 3 kHz signal runs from 7.175 up to 7.178 MHz. Subtract the bandwidth from the dial reading and you have the lower edge.

G4D09.x: Upper sideband puts energy above the displayed carrier, so 14.347 plus 3 kHz reaches 14.350 MHz, exactly the top of the band. One kilohertz higher on the dial and you would be transmitting outside it.

G4D10.x: Stay at least 3 kHz above the lower edge, because LSB energy extends downward by the full bandwidth. Sitting on the edge itself puts your sidebands outside the segment even though the dial looks legal.

G4D11.x: Stay at least 3 kHz below the upper edge, the mirror image of G4D10. USB extends upward, so the dial reading has to leave room for the whole signal. Same rule, opposite direction.

G4E01.x: A capacitance hat adds capacitance near the top of a short antenna, which raises the current in the radiating section and makes the antenna behave electrically longer. It lets you resonate without adding more loading coil.

G4E02.x: Voltage is highest at the tip of a mobile whip, and a sharp point concentrates the field enough to ionize the air. A rounded ball spreads the field over a larger radius, keeping the gradient below the level where corona forms.

G4E03.x: Run heavy-gauge fused wire directly to the battery, both leads. A 100-watt radio draws around 20 amps on peaks, and any lighter or longer path drops enough voltage to make the radio misbehave when you need it most.

G4E04.x: Accessory sockets are wired for small loads, often fused at 10 or 15 amps through thin wire. A 100-watt HF radio asks for roughly 20 amps, so the socket wiring becomes the weak point and can overheat.

G4E05.x: The antenna is the limitation. A whip a few feet long on 40 meters is a tiny fraction of a wavelength, heavily loaded, with low radiation resistance and real losses. Most of your power warms the loading coil rather than leaving the vehicle.

G4E06.src: ARRL Antenna Book; Q and bandwidth
G4E06.x: Shortening an antenna raises its Q, and high Q means narrow bandwidth. You may retune every few tens of kilohertz. That sharpness is the same property that makes a short antenna hard to match in the first place.

G4E07.x: A modern vehicle is full of noise sources: the ignition system, the alternator, and dozens of electronic control modules and switching supplies. All the listed sources are genuine contributors, so the inclusive answer applies.

G4E08.x: Cells are wired in series to build voltage and those strings are paralleled to build current, so the panel is series-parallel. Series alone would give the right voltage at too little current for charging.

G4E09.x: About 0.5 volts open circuit for a silicon cell, set by the physics of the silicon junction rather than by the cell's size. Area determines current, not voltage, which is why a 12-volt panel needs roughly 36 cells in series.

G4E10.x: In darkness the panel becomes a load rather than a source, and the battery would quietly discharge back through it overnight. A series diode conducts only the charging direction and blocks the reverse.

G4E11.x: Lithium iron phosphate cells need a controlled charge profile and a hard voltage ceiling, and a bare panel provides neither. A charge controller enforces the limits. Overcharging lithium chemistry is a fire risk, not merely bad for capacity.

G5A01.x: At resonance the two reactances are equal and opposite, so they cancel and only the resistance remains. In a series circuit that leaves a very low impedance, which is why series resonance is used to pass one frequency. Parallel resonance does the opposite.

G5A02.x: Reactance is opposition to alternating current from capacitance or inductance. Unlike resistance it dissipates nothing: energy is stored and returned each cycle. That is also why it varies with frequency while resistance does not.

G5A03.x: Reactance, specifically inductive reactance. An inductor opposes a change in current by generating a back EMF, and the faster the change the stronger the opposition.

G5A04.x: Reactance, in this case capacitive. Both capacitors and inductors oppose AC through reactance; what differs is the direction the opposition moves as frequency changes.

G5A05.x: Inductive reactance rises with frequency. The formula says it directly: XL equals 2πfL, so doubling frequency doubles reactance. An inductor passes DC easily and chokes off high frequencies, which is exactly how an RF choke works.

G5A06.x: Capacitive reactance falls as frequency rises, since frequency sits in the denominator of 1 over 2πfC. A capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies, the mirror image of an inductor. That is why bypass capacitors work.

G5A07.x: Admittance, measured in siemens. It is the reciprocal of impedance, the way conductance is the reciprocal of resistance. Useful when analysing parallel circuits, where admittances simply add.

G5A08.src: Ohm's law for AC; IEEE Std 270
G5A08.x: Impedance is the ratio of voltage to current, the AC generalization of resistance. It bundles resistance and reactance into one quantity, which is why it is expressed in ohms and why Ohm's law still applies.

G5A09.x: Ohms, the same unit as resistance and impedance. All three describe opposition to current, so they share a unit even though the underlying mechanisms differ.

G5A10.x: Transformers, LC networks and quarter-wave transmission line sections all transform impedance, so the inclusive answer is right. Which one you use depends on frequency, power and how wide a range you need to cover.

G5A11.x: X denotes reactance, written XL for inductive and XC for capacitive. R is resistance, Z is impedance, and Z combines R and X.

G5A12.x: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, so they cancel and the circuit looks purely resistive. Whether that leaves low or high impedance depends on whether the components are in series or parallel.

G5B01.x: Doubling or halving power is 3 dB, up or down. The exact figure is 3.01, and 3 dB is the single most useful number in radio. Its partner: 10 dB is a factor of ten.

G5B02.x: Branch currents add up to the total. Each parallel branch sees the same voltage and draws current according to its own resistance, so the source supplies the sum. Adding another branch always increases total current.

G5B03.x: With voltage and resistance given, use P equals E squared over R: 400 squared is 160,000, divided by 800 gives 200 watts. Reach for this form whenever the question hands you volts and ohms but no current.

G5B04.x: Volts times amps: 12 times 0.2 is 2.4 watts. The simplest form of the power formula, usable whenever both voltage and current are given.

G5B05.x: Current and resistance given, so use P equals I squared R. Seven milliamperes is 0.007 A, squared gives 0.000049, times 1250 gives 0.061 watts, or about 61 milliwatts. Watch the unit conversion; that is where this one is usually lost.

G5B06.x: Three steps. Halve 200 peak-to-peak for 100 volts peak, divide by root 2 for 70.7 volts RMS, then square and divide by 50 to get 100 watts. Power always comes from RMS, never from peak.

G5B07.x: The RMS value, root mean square. It is defined as the AC value that heats a resistor exactly as much as the same DC voltage would, which is why RMS is the figure used for every power calculation.

G5B08.x: Multiply RMS by root 2 for peak, then double it for peak-to-peak: 120 times 1.414 is 169.7, doubled gives 339.4 volts. Household 120 volts really does swing nearly 340 volts across a cycle.

G5B09.x: Divide peak by root 2: 17 over 1.414 is 12.0 volts RMS. Going from peak to RMS you always divide, so the answer must be smaller than the peak value.

G5B10.x: One dB down leaves 10 to the power of minus 0.1, which is 0.794, so about 79 percent gets through and 20.6 percent is lost. A single dB sounds trivial and is actually a fifth of your power.

G5B11.x: Exactly 1.00. An unmodulated carrier has a constant envelope, so its peak and average are the same. Ratios above 1 only appear once modulation makes the envelope vary, as with SSB speech.

G5B12.x: Rearrange P equals E squared over R into E equals the square root of P times R: 1200 times 50 is 60,000, and the square root is 245 volts RMS. That is a genuinely dangerous voltage inside a dummy load.

G5B13.x: The same, 1060 watts. Since an unmodulated carrier has a constant envelope, PEP equals average power. This is G5B11 asked with numbers instead of a ratio.

G5B14.x: Same three steps as G5B06: half of 500 is 250 volts peak, divided by root 2 gives 176.8 RMS, squared over 50 gives 625 watts. Peak-to-peak to RMS is a division by 2 root 2, or about 2.83.

G5C01.x: Mutual inductance. Alternating current in the primary creates a changing magnetic field, and that changing field induces a voltage in the secondary. Changing is essential, which is why a transformer does nothing with DC.

G5C02.x: Feeding a transformer backwards reverses its ratio, so a 4 to 1 step-down becomes a 4 to 1 step-up and the input is multiplied by four. Transformers are symmetrical; step-up and step-down describe how you wire it, not the part itself.

G5C03.x: Add the reciprocals and invert: one tenth plus one twentieth plus one fiftieth is 0.17, and one over 0.17 is 5.9 ohms. Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest resistor, so 5.9 passing that check is a good sanity test.

G5C04.x: For two resistors, product over sum is quicker: 100 times 200 is 20,000, divided by 300 gives 67 ohms. Again below the smaller of the two, as parallel combinations always are.

G5C05.x: Power in equals power out, so stepping voltage up means stepping current down. The primary of a step-up transformer therefore carries the higher current and needs the heavier wire. Follow the current, not the voltage.

G5C06.x: Output equals input times the turns ratio: 1500 over 500 is 3, and 120 times 3 is 360 volts. More turns on the secondary means a step-up, which the answer being larger than 120 confirms.

G5C07.x: Impedance transforms as the square of the turns ratio, so the turns ratio is the square root of the impedance ratio. 600 over 50 is 12, and the square root of 12 is 3.46, so about 3.5 to 1. Forgetting the square root is the classic error here.

G5C08.x: Capacitors in parallel simply add, but the units must match first. 750 picofarads is 0.75 nanofarads, so 5 plus 5 plus 0.75 gives 10.75 nanofarads. Parallel capacitors behave like parallel resistors turned upside down.

G5C09.x: Capacitors in series combine like parallel resistors, so three equal 100 microfarad units give 100 divided by 3, or 33.3 microfarads. Series capacitance is always less than the smallest capacitor.

G5C10.x: Inductors in parallel behave like resistors in parallel, so three equal 10 millihenry units give 10 divided by 3, about 3.3 millihenries. Inductors follow the resistor rules; capacitors are the ones that flip.

G5C11.x: Inductors in series add, exactly like resistors: 20 plus 50 is 70 millihenries. Pair this with G5C10 and the whole inductor family is covered, since inductors always follow the resistance rules.

G5C12.x: Two capacitors in series follow product over sum: 20 times 50 is 1000, divided by 70 gives 14.3 microfarads. Less than the smaller of the two, which is the check on every series capacitance answer.

G5C13.x: Add a capacitor in parallel, because parallel capacitances add. Putting one in series would reduce the total instead. Capacitors are backwards from resistors in both directions.

G5C14.x: Add an inductor in series, since series inductances add. This is the opposite arrangement from capacitors, which is precisely what the pair of questions G5C13 and G5C14 is testing.

G6A01.x: Stop at 10.5 volts, about 1.75 volts per cell. Below that the plates begin to sulfate in ways that do not fully reverse on the next charge, so every deep discharge permanently costs you capacity.

G6A02.x: Low internal resistance means less voltage is lost inside the battery itself, so it can deliver high current without the terminal voltage collapsing. That is what lets a battery run a 100-watt transmitter through modulation peaks.
