G6A03.x: About 0.3 volts, roughly half the silicon figure, because germanium has a smaller bandgap. That low drop is why germanium diodes still appear in sensitive detector circuits where 0.7 volts would swallow the signal.

G6A04.x: Electrolytics pack far more capacitance into a given volume than other types, thanks to an extremely thin oxide dielectric grown on the plate. The tradeoffs are polarity, leakage and a limited life, which is why they appear in power supplies rather than RF circuits.

G6A05.x: About 0.7 volts for silicon. Learn it beside germanium's 0.3: silicon is roughly double. Nothing much conducts below the threshold, which is why a couple of diodes in series make a simple voltage reference.

G6A06.src: ARRL Handbook; inductance of wound components
G6A06.x: A wire-wound resistor is a coil, so it has inductance whether you want it or not. At RF that reactance adds to the resistance in ways that shift tuning and make behaviour unpredictable. Use carbon or metal film instead.

G6A07.x: A switch has two states, so the transistor is driven to saturation (fully on) or cutoff (fully off). It passes through the linear region only in transit. Staying out of that middle region is what keeps dissipation low.

G6A08.x: Cheap. Low-voltage ceramics are mass-produced in enormous quantities, which is why they are everywhere. They are also small and non-polarized, but cost is the characteristic this question is after.

G6A09.x: The gate sits on a thin insulating oxide layer rather than touching the channel, which is what the M-O-S in the name describes: metal, oxide, semiconductor. That insulation gives near-zero gate current and also makes MOSFETs easy to destroy with static.

G6A10.x: The control grid. A small voltage on it steers the electron stream from cathode to plate, which is how a tube amplifies. It plays the same role the base does in a bipolar transistor.

G6A11.x: Every inductor has stray capacitance between its turns, and above the frequency where the two resonate the capacitance dominates. The part stops behaving like an inductor and starts behaving like a capacitor, which is why a choke chosen for the wrong band does nothing useful.

G6A12.x: The screen grid sits between control grid and plate and shields one from the other, cutting grid-to-plate capacitance. That capacitance is what causes unwanted feedback and oscillation in a triode amplifier.

G6B01.src: Ferrite material science; manufacturer mix data
G6B01.x: A ferrite's mix, its exact material composition, determines the frequency range where it is lossy and therefore useful. A mix meant for HF does little at VHF. Choosing the right mix matters more than adding more turns.

G6B02.x: Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuit: a complete microwave amplifier or mixer built on a single chip. Monolithic means one piece of substrate, which keeps the internal connections short enough to work at those frequencies.

G6B03.src: CMOS logic; IEEE logic family standards
G6B03.x: CMOS draws almost no current when it is not switching, because its complementary transistors are never both fully on. TTL pulls current continuously. That difference is why battery-powered devices use CMOS.

G6B04.x: About 4 GHz for 50-ohm BNC. Above that the connector's geometry no longer maintains constant impedance and SWR climbs. Keep the connector ladder straight: BNC to 4 GHz, SMA to several GHz, Type N to 10 GHz.

G6B05.x: A toroid confines its magnetic field almost entirely within the core, so it needs fewer turns for a given inductance and barely couples to neighbouring components. All the listed advantages are real, so the inclusive answer applies.

G6B06.x: An op-amp is an analog device. It amplifies continuously varying voltages rather than switching between logic levels. Digital circuits deal in discrete states; the op-amp works with everything in between.

G6B07.x: Type N is the weatherproof one, holding a constant 50-ohm impedance up to about 10 GHz. That combination of sealing and controlled impedance is why it belongs at the top of a tower rather than a PL-259.

G6B08.x: Forward biased. Current crossing the junction in the forward direction releases energy as photons. Reverse the polarity and it simply stops, since an LED is a diode first and a light second.

G6B10.x: The bead adds impedance to common-mode current, the component travelling the same direction on shield and centre conductor together. The differential signal you want sees almost nothing, so the bead removes the problem without touching your transmission.

G6B11.x: SMA is a small threaded connector good for several gigahertz, common on handhelds and test gear. Its size is the point: it fits where a Type N cannot, at the cost of lower power handling and a finite number of matings.

G6B12.x: RCA phono connectors handle low-frequency and DC connections on the back of a transceiver: keying lines, ALC, audio. They are cheap and easy but have no controlled impedance, so they never carry RF.

G7A01.x: A bleeder resistor drains the filter capacitors once power is removed, so the supply is not still holding a lethal charge when you open it. It draws a trickle continuously in exchange for making the chassis safe to work on.

G7A02.x: Capacitors and inductors. The capacitor holds voltage up between rectifier pulses while the inductor resists changes in current, and together they smooth pulsating DC into something steady. Resistors would only waste power doing it.

G7A03.x: That is the classic full-wave centre-tapped circuit: each diode handles one half of the cycle, using the centre tap as the return. Two diodes and a centre tap means full-wave; four diodes in a bridge is the other way to get there.

G7A04.x: A half-wave rectifier needs just one diode, which is its only real advantage. It throws away half the cycle, so the filtering has to work much harder and the transformer is used less efficiently.

G7A05.x: 180 degrees, half the cycle. The diode conducts on one polarity and blocks the other, so only half the waveform reaches the load. That leaves a long gap the filter capacitor has to cover.

G7A06.x: All 360 degrees. A full-wave circuit flips the negative half up rather than discarding it, so both halves reach the load. Nothing is wasted, which is why full-wave supplies filter more easily.

G7A07.x: DC pulses at twice the input frequency. Both halves of each cycle become a positive pulse, so 60 Hz in gives 120 pulses per second out. That doubled ripple frequency is easier to filter, which is a second advantage of full-wave.

G7A08.x: A switchmode supply chops the input at tens of kilohertz or more, and transformers and filters shrink dramatically as frequency rises. That is why a switching supply weighs a fraction of a linear one at the same power. The cost is switching noise.

G7A09.x: Symbol 1 shows a circle with a vertical bar for the gate and an arrow into the channel, with the gate not touching the channel line. That separation is the FET signature. Compare it with symbol 2, where the leads meet the base bar directly.

G7A10.x: Symbol 5 is the diode whose cathode bar is bent at the ends rather than straight, which marks a Zener. The bend is the only difference from the plain diode at symbol 3, so look closely at the bar.

G7A11.x: Symbol 2 is the bipolar transistor, and the arrow on the emitter points away from the base, which makes it NPN. An arrow pointing inward would be PNP. Remember it as Not Pointing iN.

G7A12.x: Symbol 6 shows two coils with solid lines drawn between them, and those lines represent an iron or solid core. Air-core transformers omit them, so the presence of the core lines is what the question is testing.

G7A13.x: Symbol 7 is the coil with an extra connection partway along its length. A tap lets you take part of the winding, so one inductor offers several values. No arrow means fixed taps rather than a continuously variable inductor.

G7B01.x: Neutralizing cancels the feedback that internal capacitance couples from output back to input. Left alone that feedback turns an amplifier into an oscillator, so a deliberate out-of-phase path is injected to cancel it.

G7B02.x: Class C is the most efficient, because the device conducts for well under half the cycle and dissipates very little the rest of the time. Efficiency and linearity trade against each other, so Class C is also the most distorting.

G7B03.x: AND means both. The output goes high only when every input is high, so with two inputs there is exactly one combination that produces a high output. OR would need only one input high.

G7B04.x: 100 percent. A Class A stage conducts through the entire cycle, which is what makes it the most linear and the least efficient. The device dissipates power even with no signal present.

G7B05.x: Eight, since 2 to the third power is 8. Each bit doubles the count, so n bits gives 2 to the n states: 3 bits gives 8, 4 bits gives 16. The counter runs 000 through 111.

G7B06.x: A shift register is a chain of clocked stages, each passing its contents to the next on every clock pulse. Data walks along the array one step per clock, which is how serial and parallel formats get converted.

G7B07.x: An amplifier and a frequency-selective filter connected in a feedback loop. The amplifier supplies gain, the filter decides which frequency survives, and the loop sustains oscillation at that frequency.

G7B08.x: RF output power divided by DC input power. A 100-watt output drawing 200 watts from the supply is 50 percent efficient, and the missing 100 watts left as heat. The difference always becomes heat, which is why amplifiers need sinks and fans.

G7B09.x: The inductance and capacitance of the tank circuit set the frequency, since resonance occurs where their reactances cancel. Change either component and the frequency moves, which is exactly how a VFO tunes.

G7B10.x: A linear amplifier reproduces the input waveform's shape at higher amplitude, without adding distortion. That fidelity is essential for SSB, where the envelope carries the information. Class A and AB are linear; Class C is not.

G7B11.x: FM, because its envelope is constant. Class C mangles amplitude but FM carries nothing in the amplitude, so nothing is lost and you keep the efficiency. Try it with SSB and the signal is destroyed.

G7C01.x: A filter. A balanced modulator produces both sidebands with the carrier suppressed, and a sharp filter then passes one sideband and rejects the other. Filter method is the traditional way to generate SSB.

G7C02.x: Double-sideband RF with the carrier suppressed. The balancing is what kills the carrier; both sidebands survive. Removing one of them is the next stage, which is what G7C01 asks about.

G7C03.x: To present the impedance both the transmitter and the feed line expect, normally 50 ohms. The transmitter delivers full power into its designed load, and reflections on the line are minimized.

G7C04.x: A product detector mixes the incoming SSB signal with a locally generated carrier to recover the audio. SSB arrives with its carrier removed, so the receiver has to supply a replacement, and that is what the detector multiplies against.

G7C05.x: A DDS synthesizes any frequency you ask for from a single crystal reference, so you get continuous tuning with crystal stability. Older VFOs gave you one or the other, not both.

G7C06.x: A DSP filter is defined in software, so its bandwidth and response shape are just numbers you can change. One radio offers dozens of filters where an analog design would need a physical crystal filter for each.

G7C07.x: Insertion loss is the attenuation a filter adds inside its own passband, the price you pay for the signals you wanted to keep. Ideally near zero, and it is measured by comparing the signal with and without the filter in circuit.

G7C08.x: Sensitivity depends on noise figure, gain distribution and bandwidth together, so all the listed parameters matter. Sensitivity is a system property rather than a single stage's specification.

G7C09.x: Ninety degrees, which is what quadrature means. Two signals a quarter cycle apart carry both amplitude and phase, and that pair is enough to describe any modulation completely.

G7C10.x: With both I and Q available, any modulation can be created or decoded purely in software, since the pair fully describes amplitude and phase. That is why one SDR handles SSB, FM, digital modes and anything invented next year.

G7C11.x: An SDR does filtering, demodulation and modulation in software, so all the listed functions apply. The hardware's job shrinks to converting between RF and digital samples as faithfully as possible.

G7C12.x: Cutoff frequency, defined at the half-power point, which is 3 dB down. Half power is not zero power: a low-pass filter keeps attenuating above cutoff rather than stopping abruptly there.

G7C13.x: Ultimate rejection is the best attenuation a filter achieves far outside its passband. Insertion loss describes what happens inside the passband, ultimate rejection describes what happens well outside it.

G7C14.x: Between the upper and lower half-power points, each 3 dB down from the peak. Same convention as the cutoff frequency in G7C12. Bandwidth is the distance between those two 3 dB points.

G8A01.x: Direct FSK shifts the oscillator itself between two frequencies under control of the data bits. No audio tones are involved, which distinguishes it from AFSK, where tones are fed into an SSB transmitter instead.

G8A02.x: Phase modulation, PM. Information rides on where the wave sits in its cycle rather than on how fast or how strong it is. PM and FM are closely related, which is why radios often list the mode as FM/PM together.

G8A03.x: Frequency modulation. The instantaneous frequency moves with the modulating signal while amplitude stays constant. That constant amplitude is what gives FM its noise immunity and lets Class C amplifiers handle it.

G8A04.x: Phase modulation. A reactance modulator applied at an RF amplifier stage varies phase rather than the oscillator's frequency. Applied to the oscillator itself it would produce FM, so where it sits determines which you get.

G8A05.x: Amplitude modulation. The instantaneous power level tracks the modulating signal, which is exactly why AM is vulnerable to noise: anything that changes amplitude along the way corrupts the information.

G8A06.x: QPSK31 uses four phase states, includes forward error correction, and occupies the same narrow bandwidth as PSK31. All the listed characteristics are accurate, so the inclusive answer applies. The FEC costs throughput but survives worse paths.

G8A07.x: Single sideband, about 3 kHz. AM needs roughly 6 kHz for the same audio because it carries both sidebands plus a carrier, and FM voice needs 10 to 15 kHz. SSB is the narrowest phone mode there is.

G8A08.x: Excessive bandwidth. Driving a transmitter past its linear range creates distortion products that spread outside the intended channel, so you splatter onto neighbouring frequencies. It also makes your audio worse, not louder.

G8A09.x: FT8 uses 8-tone frequency shift keying, which is where the 8 in the name comes from. Eight tones let each symbol carry three bits, and the whole signal fits in about 50 Hz.

G8A10.x: Flat-topping is what you see when the modulation peaks get clipped off square because drive or speech level is too high. The envelope should be a smooth curve; a flattened top means distortion and splatter.

G8A11.x: The envelope is the curve you get by joining the peaks of the modulated waveform. It traces out the modulating audio, which is why looking at the envelope on a scope tells you immediately whether the modulation is clean.

G8A12.x: QPSK uses four phase states at 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees, and four states encode two bits each. That doubles the data rate compared with plain PSK without needing more bandwidth.

G8A13.src: Link budget analysis; ITU-R Rec. P.341
G8A13.x: A link budget adds up transmit power and antenna gains, subtracts every loss along the path, and tells you what arrives at the receiver. It is how you decide whether a path will work before building anything.

G8A14.x: Link margin is the headroom: how much stronger the received signal is than the minimum the receiver needs. Margin is what absorbs fading, so a path with no margin works only under ideal conditions.

G8B01.x: The local oscillator. Tuning it changes which incoming frequency lands on the fixed IF, so the LO is what you move when you turn the dial. The IF stays put, which is what lets its filters be so good.

G8B02.x: Image response. A signal offset from the desired one by twice the IF mixes down to the same IF, so the receiver cannot tell them apart. Front-end filtering ahead of the mixer is what rejects it.

G8B03.x: Heterodyning, from the Greek for other force. Mixing two frequencies in a non-linear device produces their sum and difference, and that principle underlies every superheterodyne receiver.

G8B04.x: A multiplier stage. It is driven into non-linearity deliberately so it generates harmonics, then one harmonic is filtered out. That is how a stable low-frequency oscillator reaches VHF, and it is why G8B07's deviation gets multiplied too.

G8B05.x: Odd-order products land closest to the original signals, which is precisely why they cause trouble. Third-order products such as 2F1 minus F2 fall right beside the wanted signals, where no filter can remove them.

G8B06.x: Carson's rule: bandwidth is twice the sum of deviation and highest modulating frequency. Two times 5 plus 3 gives 16 kHz. Both numbers go inside the parentheses before doubling, which is the step people skip.

G8B07.x: 146.52 divided by 12.21 is exactly 12, so the oscillator is multiplied twelvefold. Deviation multiplies by the same factor, so working backwards gives 5000 divided by 12, or 416.7 Hz at the oscillator.

G8B08.x: Modes differ enormously in duty cycle. SSB transmits in bursts, while FT8 and RTTY key at full output for their entire transmission. Run a high duty cycle mode at full power and you can cook a transmitter rated for SSB service.

G8B09.x: Noise arrives across the whole passband while the signal occupies only part of it, so a filter matched to the mode admits the signal and rejects the rest. Matching bandwidth to mode gives the best signal-to-noise ratio available.

G8B10.x: Higher symbol rates need more bandwidth. Faster transitions mean sidebands spread further from the carrier, which is a hard limit set by information theory rather than by equipment quality.

G8B11.x: Both the sum and the difference appear, along with the two originals. The IF filter then selects whichever you want, which is why the same mixer works for either high-side or low-side injection.

G8B12.x: Intermodulation. Two signals passing through a non-linear stage mix with each other and produce sums and differences of their multiples. Unlike harmonics, these products involve both signals, which is why they land in awkward places.

G8B13.x: Order is the sum of the coefficients, so 2F1 minus F2 has order 2 plus 1, which is 3 and therefore odd. Third-order products are the troublesome ones because they fall closest to the original frequencies.

G8C02.x: WSPR, the Weak Signal Propagation Reporter, runs a few watts or less and reports decodes to a central database. It is built to map propagation rather than to hold contacts, so you can see which paths are open worldwide.

G8C03.x: The header carries source and destination call signs plus the digipeater path, so every station handling the frame knows where it came from and where it is going. The data payload follows, and a checksum ends the frame.

G8C04.src: ITU-T Rec. F.1 (International Telegraph Alphabet No. 2)
G8C04.x: Baudot is a 5-bit code with start and stop bits added around each character. Five bits give only 32 combinations, so it uses shift characters to switch between letters and figures, which is why RTTY garbles into numbers when a shift is missed.

G8C05.x: NAK is a negative acknowledgment: the block arrived corrupted, so send it again. Its counterpart ACK confirms good receipt. That request-and-resend cycle is what the ARQ in the name describes.

G8C06.x: After enough failed retries the connection is dropped. The protocol will not corrupt your data by giving up on accuracy, so when the path degrades past usefulness it disconnects instead.

G8C07.x: FT8 decodes well below the noise floor, roughly to minus 21 dB signal-to-noise. It achieves that with a tightly structured message, a fixed 15-second window and heavy error correction, trading flexibility for sensitivity.

G8C08.x: Varicode gives common characters short bit sequences and rare ones longer sequences, and upper case letters are among the long ones. Typing in capitals genuinely slows your transmission, which is why PSK31 operators use lower case.

G8C09.x: A mesh finds another route when a node fails, because every node relays for its neighbours and the routing adapts. That self-healing property is the reason mesh networks suit emergency work.

G8C10.x: FEC sends extra redundant bits alongside the data, enough that the receiver can reconstruct what was corrupted without asking for a resend. That is the difference from ARQ, which requests retransmission instead.

G8C11.x: Mark and space, the two frequencies of an FSK signal. The names come from mechanical telegraphy, where one state marked the paper and the other left a space. Swap them and the decode inverts into garbage.

G8C12.x: Varicode, a variable-length code designed for PSK31. Assigning the shortest patterns to the most frequent letters keeps the average throughput high at a very low symbol rate, which is what makes PSK31 so narrow.

G8C13.x: Extra vertical lines flanking the signal are the sidebands overmodulation creates. A clean data signal shows only its own tones, so those flanking lines mean turn the audio down.

G8C14.x: A waterfall maps frequency across the screen, signal strength as brightness or colour, and time scrolling vertically. That third axis is what makes it a waterfall rather than a plain spectrum display.

G8C15.x: FT8 reports signal-to-noise ratio referenced to a 2.5 kHz bandwidth, so plus 3 means the signal is 3 dB above the noise in that reference. Negative numbers are the norm; anything positive is genuinely strong for FT8.

G8C16.src: ETSI TS 102 361 (DMR); JARL D-STAR; Yaesu System Fusion
G8C16.x: DMR, D-STAR and System Fusion are the three digital voice systems in common amateur use, each with its own vocoder and network. They do not interoperate over the air, which is why local repeater choice matters.

G9A01.x: For parallel conductors, impedance is set by the spacing between conductor centres and the conductor radius. Wider spacing raises it, thicker wire lowers it. Nothing about length or power enters into characteristic impedance.

G9A02.x: High SWR only matters in a lossy line. Reflected power travels the line again, so it gets attenuated twice more, and each pass costs whatever that cable loses per hundred feet. On low-loss line at HF the penalty is small; on lossy cable at UHF it is severe.

G9A03.x: 450 ohms. Window line is the flat ladder line with rectangular cutouts, and those windows keep the effective dielectric mostly air, which is why its loss is far lower than coax.

G9A04.x: A mismatch between the line's characteristic impedance and the antenna's feed point impedance. Whatever the line cannot deliver into that load comes back toward the transmitter. Match the two and nothing reflects.

G9A05.x: Attenuation rises with frequency. Skin effect crowds current into an ever thinner surface layer, raising resistance, and dielectric losses climb too. A cable that is fine on 80 meters can waste half your power at 440 MHz.

G9A06.x: Decibels per 100 feet, quoted at a stated frequency. Expressing it per unit length lets you scale to your own run, and it must be per frequency because loss changes with it.

G9A07.x: Match the antenna feed point impedance to the line's characteristic impedance. Standing waves exist because energy reflects, and only a matched load absorbs it all. A tuner at the shack end does not prevent them.

G9A08.x: Still 5:1. The tuner makes the transmitter see 1:1, but nothing at the antenna has changed, so the standing waves on the line are exactly where they were. This is the most commonly misunderstood point about tuners.

G9A09.x: For a purely resistive load, SWR is the ratio of the larger impedance to the smaller: 200 over 50 is 4, so 4:1. Always put the bigger number on top, since SWR can never read below 1:1.

G9A10.x: 50 over 10 is 5, so 5:1. Note this is a load below the line impedance while G9A09 was above it, and the arithmetic is the same either way. Divide larger by smaller.

G9A11.x: Loss makes the SWR measured at the shack look better than it really is. The reflected wave is attenuated on its way back, so less of it reaches your meter. A very lossy line can read a comfortable SWR while the antenna is badly mismatched.

G9B01.x: A random wire fed directly against the station gives the RF current no defined return path, so it flows on your equipment chassis, cables and microphone. That is what causes RF burns and interference in your own shack. A counterpoise or proper ground system is what fixes it.

G9B02.x: Slope the radials downward. A quarter-wave ground plane with horizontal radials feeds near 36 ohms; drooping them raises it toward 50, which matches coax directly. Around 45 degrees gets you there.

G9B03.x: Omnidirectional in azimuth, meaning equal in every compass direction. It is not omnidirectional in elevation: the pattern is a doughnut with a null straight up, which is why verticals favour low angles and DX.

G9B04.x: A figure-eight broadside to the wire, with deep nulls off the ends. Point the wire across the path you want rather than at it. Two lobes at right angles to the conductor is the whole pattern.

G9B05.x: Below half a wavelength up, ground reflection fills in the dipole's nulls at high elevation angles, so the azimuthal pattern goes nearly omnidirectional. The figure-eight only appears once the antenna is high enough to be free of that effect.

G9B06.x: On the surface or a few inches under. Radials work as the return path for antenna current, and burying them deeply puts lossy soil between them and the antenna. Shallow is better, and more radials beat longer ones.

G9B07.x: It steadily decreases. A dipole is near 73 ohms in free space, but bringing it close to ground drops the feed point impedance well below that, sometimes under 50 ohms at a tenth of a wavelength. Ground coupling changes the antenna, not just the pattern.

G9B08.x: It steadily increases, because current is highest at the centre and voltage is highest at the ends. Impedance is voltage over current, so moving toward the ends raises it, reaching thousands of ohms at the tip. That is why an end-fed half wave needs a matching network.

G9B09.x: Lower ground losses. A vertical relies on the ground as part of its return path, so soil conductivity directly costs you efficiency. A horizontal antenna a reasonable height up does not depend on the ground that way.

G9B10.x: Use 468 divided by the frequency in MHz: 468 over 14.25 is 32.8, so about 33 feet. The 468 accounts for end effect, which is why it is not the full 492 that free-space geometry would suggest.

G9B11.x: 468 divided by 3.55 gives 131.8, so about 132 feet. Same formula as G9B10, and worth noticing that a lower frequency means a much longer antenna. Eighty meters needs real estate.

G9B12.x: A quarter wave uses 234, half of the dipole's 468: 234 over 28.5 is 8.2, so about 8 feet. Two formulas cover most antenna length questions, and one is simply half the other.

G9C01.x: Larger-diameter elements. Fatter conductors lower the antenna's Q, and lower Q means a broader response. It is the same relationship that makes a physically short, heavily loaded antenna so narrow.

G9C02.x: About a half wavelength, since the driven element is essentially a dipole. The reflector and directors are parasitic: they are not fed at all, and they work by re-radiating what the driven element illuminates them with.

G9C03.x: Reflector longer, director shorter. A longer element is inductive and lags, pushing energy forward; a shorter one is capacitive and leads, pulling it forward. Directors always point the way the beam looks.

G9C04.x: dBi is 2.15 dB higher for the same antenna, because an isotropic radiator is a weaker reference than a dipole. A dipole already has 2.15 dBi of gain, so quoting against isotropic makes any number look better. Check which reference a manufacturer used.

G9C05.x: Gain increases. A longer boom with more directors concentrates radiation into a narrower beam, and narrowing the beam is what gain means. The cost is a sharper pattern and less bandwidth.

G9C07.x: Front-to-back ratio compares power in the main lobe with power radiated directly behind. It measures how well the antenna ignores what is behind you, which matters more for rejecting interference than for reaching the station in front.

G9C08.x: The main lobe is the direction of maximum radiated field strength, the direction you point the beam. Every other lobe is a side lobe, and gain figures always refer to the main one.

G9C09.src: Antenna stacking theory; ARRL Antenna Book
G9C09.x: About 3 dB higher, because doubling the number of identical antennas doubles the effective aperture. Stacking two of anything correctly phased is the classic 3 dB, the same 3 dB that means twice the power.

G9C10.x: Element lengths, element spacing and the matching arrangement all interact, so any of them can be adjusted to favour gain, front-to-back ratio or bandwidth. Since all the listed items apply, the inclusive answer is right. You cannot maximize all three at once.

G9C11.x: A beta or hairpin match is a shorted stub across the feed point, adding a parallel inductance that transforms a low driven-element impedance up to 50 ohms. It is simple, weatherproof and needs no adjustment once cut.

G9C12.x: A gamma match feeds the element off-centre through a series capacitor, so the driven element can stay bonded to the boom. That mechanical simplicity is the advantage: no insulators to fail up in the air.

G9D01.x: A horizontal dipole between a tenth and a quarter wavelength up. That low height sends most of the energy nearly straight upward, which is exactly what NVIS needs to drop signals back down within a few hundred miles.

G9D02.x: Very high, in the thousands of ohms, because voltage peaks and current is minimal at the end of a half wave. That is the same current and voltage distribution behind G9B08, which is why an end fed needs a substantial matching transformer.

G9D03.x: Omnidirectional in the plane of the halo. A halo is a dipole bent into a near-circle, which keeps horizontal polarization for weak-signal work while giving coverage in all directions rather than a figure-eight.

G9D04.x: Traps enable multiband operation. Each trap is a parallel resonant circuit that goes high-impedance on one band, electrically disconnecting the wire beyond it, so the same antenna presents a different length on each band.

G9D05.x: It narrows the main lobe in elevation. Vertical stacking compresses the pattern vertically, which lowers the takeoff angle and puts more energy toward the horizon where distant stations are. Horizontal coverage is unchanged.

G9D06.x: Wide bandwidth. A log-periodic covers a very broad frequency range with usable gain and pattern, which is why it appears where one antenna must handle many bands. The tradeoff is less gain than a monoband Yagi of similar size.

G9D07.x: Element lengths and spacings scale logarithmically along the boom, so at any frequency a different group of elements is active. That scaling is what produces the wide bandwidth in G9D06.

G9D08.x: By varying the base loading inductance. A motor drives a threaded core in and out of the coil, which is where the screwdriver nickname comes from. It lets one mobile antenna retune across the bands from the driver's seat.

G9D09.x: Directional receiving on MF and low HF. A Beverage is a long wire close to the ground, terminated at the far end, and it is a receiving antenna: very directional, very quiet, and inefficient enough that nobody transmits on one.

G9D10.src: ARRL Antenna Book; small loop theory
G9D10.x: Nulls broadside to the loop, with maximum response in the plane of the loop. Those nulls are extremely sharp, which is what makes a small loop the standard tool for direction finding and for notching out a noise source.

G9D11.x: Poor harmonic rejection. An antenna resonant on several bands is also happy to radiate on harmonics that fall on those bands, so anything spurious your transmitter produces gets radiated efficiently rather than being attenuated.

G9D12.x: An inverted V. One central support with both legs sloping down is cheaper and needs less space than a flat dipole. The sloping legs narrow the pattern slightly and lower the feed point impedance a little.

T0A01.x: A lead-acid battery can deliver hundreds of amps into a dead short. A dropped wrench across the terminals will glow red, spray molten metal, and can rupture the case. Lead-acid also vents hydrogen, so an arc near a charging battery risks an explosion.

T0A02.src: IEC 60479 (effects of current on the human body)
T0A02.x: Current through the body can burn tissue, disrupt breathing, and stop the heart through ventricular fibrillation. All three are real, so the inclusive answer is right. Current is what injures you, which is why fairly low voltages can still kill.

T0A03.x: In US practice black insulation marks the hot conductor. White is neutral and green or bare is ground. Treat any black or red wire as live until you have proven otherwise with a meter.

T0A04.x: A fuse is a deliberate weak point that opens when current climbs past its rating, cutting power before the wiring overheats. It protects the circuit and the building, not the equipment plugged into it.

T0A05.x: The fuse rating is chosen for the wire behind it. Fit a 20-amp fuse to wiring sized for 5 amps and the fuse will happily pass current that overheats the conductors, so the wiring becomes the fuse. That is how electrical fires start.

T0A06.x: Good practice stacks up: bond equipment to a common ground, use three-wire cords, and disconnect power before working inside a chassis. All the listed measures are sound, so the inclusive answer is correct.

T0A07.x: Mount the arrester on a grounded panel where the feed lines enter the building. Bleeding the surge to ground at the entry point keeps it out of the shack. An arrester deep inside the house has already let the strike travel past everything you wanted to protect.

T0A08.x: In series with the hot conductor only. Interrupting the hot line stops current and leaves the equipment at ground potential. Fusing the neutral instead could open it while the chassis stays connected to a live hot wire, which is worse than no fuse.

T0A09.x: Bond every ground rod and earth connection together with heavy wire or strap. Separate grounds sitting at different potentials during a surge will push current through your equipment as it equalizes. One bonded system, not several isolated ones.

T0A10.x: Fast charging or discharging generates heat and drives the chemistry harder than it is meant to go, producing gas inside the cell. Lead-acid vents hydrogen; lithium cells can go into thermal runaway. Overheating and out-gassing are the hazards.

T0A11.x: Filter capacitors hold their charge after the power is off, sometimes at lethal voltage for a long time. Switching off is not the same as being safe. Verify with a meter and discharge through a resistor before reaching inside.

T0A12.x: Both the meter and its leads have voltage ratings, and the leads are usually the weak link. Using probes rated below the voltage you are measuring risks flashover to your hands. Confirm the rating covers the circuit before you touch anything.

T0B01.x: Keep ground conductors short and direct. A lightning surge rises so fast that the conductor's inductance dominates, and every extra foot or bend adds impedance that pushes the surge to find another route, possibly through your equipment.

T0B02.src: OSHA 1926 Subpart M; ARRL Antenna Book
T0B02.x: Climbing requires a proper climbing harness, a helper or observer on the ground, and gear inspected before use. All the listed requirements are genuine, so the inclusive answer is right.

T0B03.x: Never. There is no tower short enough or job quick enough to make solo climbing acceptable. If something goes wrong up there, an observer on the ground is the only thing standing between an accident and a fatality.

T0B04.x: Look for overhead power lines and stay clear of them. A tower section or antenna being raised is a long conductor swinging through the air, and contact with a distribution line is usually fatal. Survey the site before anything goes up.

T0B05.x: Wire through the turnbuckle body stops it from unwinding as wind vibration works it loose over months. Guy tension slowly slackens otherwise, and a loose guy lets the tower move in ways it was never designed to.

T0B06.src: ARRL Antenna Book; OSHA clearance guidance
T0B06.x: Site the antenna so that if the whole thing falls, no part reaches within 10 feet of the power wires. Plan for the failure, not just the installation. Height plus guy radius decides how far away that has to be.

T0B07.src: ARRL Antenna Book; manufacturer safety guidance
T0B07.x: Never climb a crank-up tower unless it is fully retracted or mechanical locks are in place. The cable is the only thing holding the sections apart, and a cable failure with a climber aboard turns the tower into a guillotine.

T0B08.x: Give each tower leg its own eight-foot ground rod, then bond the rods to the tower and to each other. Multiple paths share the surge current, and bonding keeps every part of the system at the same potential while it happens.

T0B09.x: Utility poles carry high-voltage lines, and the pole is the utility's property besides. Climbing one or attaching hardware puts you within reach of conductors that will kill you long before you touch them.

T0B10.x: Avoid sharp bends. A fast surge does not follow a tight corner well, and the added inductance can make it jump the bend to something nearby. Sweeping curves keep the current on the conductor you chose for it.

T0B11.x: Local electrical codes govern grounding, generally adopting the National Electrical Code. The FCC regulates your transmissions, not your wiring, so grounding requirements come from the locality rather than Part 97.

T0C01.x: Radio waves are non-ionizing. Their photons lack the energy to strip electrons from atoms, so RF cannot ionize tissue the way X-rays or gamma rays do. Its effect at high levels is heating, which is what the exposure rules are written around.

T0C02.x: The 30 to 300 MHz range has the most restrictive limits, so of these bands 50 MHz is the answer. The human body is roughly resonant at those frequencies, absorbing energy most efficiently, so the allowable exposure is set lowest there.

T0C03.x: Exposure limits are averaged over time, so transmitting half as much doubles the power density you may produce. Drop from 100 percent to 50 percent duty cycle and the allowable density goes up by a factor of two.

T0C04.x: Power, frequency, antenna gain and pattern, and how close people get all feed into the exposure calculation, along with duty cycle. Every listed factor genuinely matters, so the inclusive answer is right.

T0C05.x: The body absorbs RF more efficiently at some frequencies than others, peaking where a person is about a half wavelength tall. Limits are tightened where absorption is greatest, which is why the VHF range is the most restrictive.

T0C06.x: You may use the FCC's calculation tables, run the equations yourself, or measure with calibrated field-strength equipment. All are acceptable, so the inclusive answer applies. OET Bulletin 65 is the document that lays out the methods.

T0C07.x: Touching a radiating antenna concentrates RF current at the contact point and produces a burn that is deep and slow to heal. It happens at surprisingly modest power. Mount antennas where nobody can reach them while you transmit.

T0C08.x: Move the antennas. Exposure falls steeply with distance, so relocating an antenna farther from people is usually more effective than cutting power, and it costs you nothing on the air.

T0C09.x: Re-evaluate whenever anything in the transmitter or antenna system changes. A new amplifier, a different antenna, or a relocated feed point all alter the exposure picture, so the original evaluation no longer describes your station.

T0C10.x: The limits are based on average exposure over a period, not on peak power. A transmitter sending half the time delivers half the average energy, so duty cycle scales the exposure directly.

T0C11.x: Duty cycle is the percentage of the averaging period during which the transmitter is actually transmitting. SSB and CW have low duty cycles because you are receiving much of the time; FM and digital modes run far higher.

T0C12.x: Ionizing radiation carries enough energy per photon to break chemical bonds and damage DNA directly. RF does not come close, so its only established hazard at high levels is heating. Different mechanism entirely, not simply a weaker version.

T0C13.x: The station licensee. Section 97.13(c) puts the duty on the licensee before allowing the station to transmit, and §97.103(a) makes the licensee responsible for proper operation generally. It does not shift to the control operator or the equipment maker.

T1A01.x: Section 97.1 lists five principles behind the amateur service. Paragraph (c) is the one tested here: the rules provide for "advancing skills in both the communication and technical phases of the art." On the exam, look for the choice that names skills and covers both sides of the hobby, operating and technical. That pairing is the giveaway.

T1A02.x: The FCC writes Part 97 and enforces it. Every rule on this exam traces back to the Commission. Any question asking who regulates, licenses, or enforces amateur radio in the United States has the same answer.

T1A03.x: Voice identification must be in English, and the rule adds that "use of a phonetic alphabet as an aid for correct station identification is encouraged." Encouraged is the word to spot. Pair "encouraged" with "phone emissions" and you have the answer.

T1A04.x: Section 97.23 requires your license grant to carry an email address where you can receive electronic correspondence. That is the channel the FCC uses: an email with a link to download your grant. Two things to hold onto for the exam. It comes from the FCC, and it arrives electronically.

T1A05.x: A control operator must be a person "for whom an amateur operator/primary station license grant appears on the ULS consolidated licensee database." The ULS entry is the proof. Until your grant posts there you are not licensed to transmit, whatever paperwork you are holding.

T1A06.x: Section 97.203(d) lists the segments where a beacon may run under automatic control. The only HF one is 28.200 to 28.300 MHz on ten meters. Memorize that range. Worth carrying alongside it: §97.203(c) caps beacon power at 100 watts.

T1A07.x: Straight from the definitions: "Space station. An amateur station located more than 50 km above the Earth's surface." Altitude is the entire definition. Fifty kilometers is the number to remember, and how the station got up there does not enter into it.

T1A08.x: A frequency coordinator is an entity recognized by local amateurs "that recommends transmit/receive channels and associated operating and technical parameters" for repeater and auxiliary stations. Recommends, not assigns. The answer you want is the one built around recommending channels.

T1A09.x: Same definition, other half of the sentence. A coordinator is one "recognized in a local or regional area by amateur operators whose stations are eligible to be auxiliary or repeater stations." When the question asks who selects a coordinator, look for the choice describing local amateurs rather than any national organization.

T1A10.x: No station may transmit in RACES unless it "is certified by a civil defense organization as registered with that organization." Your operator license alone is not enough. The exam is testing that second piece: enrollment with the served civil defense organization, in place beforehand.

T1A11.x: One sentence: "No amateur operator shall willfully or maliciously interfere with or cause interference to any radio communication or signal." Willful or malicious is the exam language and it matches the answer nearly word for word.

T1B01.x: Technicians get one slice of HF phone: 28.300 to 28.500 MHz on ten meters. The rest of the Technician HF allocation is CW and data only. Learn the pair 28.300 and 28.500 as your phone window and this question and T1B06 both fall out of it.

T1B02.x: Working the ISS happens on 2 meters and 70 centimeters, and Technicians hold full privileges on both. Section 97.207(a) adds that any class of operator may work a space station within the privileges they hold. No upgrade required.

T1B03.x: The 6-meter band runs 50.0 to 54.0 MHz, so 52.525 MHz sits inside it. That frequency is also the national FM simplex calling channel on 6 meters, which makes it easy to remember.

T1B04.x: The 2-meter band is 144 to 148 MHz, so 146.52 MHz falls in it. You will meet 146.52 constantly: it is the national FM simplex calling frequency. Knowing that one number answers this question without doing any band math.

T1B05.x: Technicians may run digital modes on all of their HF, VHF and UHF allocations, subject to the emission types §97.305 authorizes for each segment. When a question lists several Technician bands and asks where digital is allowed, the answer is usually all of them.

T1B06.x: Ten meters is the only HF band where a Technician may use phone, in the 28.300 to 28.500 MHz segment. The Technician allocations on 80, 40 and 15 meters are CW and data only. One HF band for voice, and it is 10 meters.

T1B07.x: The bottom 100 kHz of both 6 meters and 2 meters is reserved for CW: 50.0 to 50.1 MHz and 144.0 to 144.1 MHz. These are the weak-signal segments where operators work long-haul contacts, and voice would swamp them. Remember it as the first 100 kHz of each band.

T1B08.x: Where amateur radio is secondary, another service holds the primary allocation. You may transmit there, but you must not interfere with the primary users and you have to accept interference from them. Secondary means you yield, not that the segment is off limits.

T1B09.x: Your emitted signal occupies bandwidth on both sides of the dial reading, and neither your display nor the far end is perfectly calibrated. Sitting right on the edge can push sidebands outside the band. Section 97.101(a) requires good engineering and good amateur practice, so leave yourself margin.

T1B10.x: Every amateur band above 50 MHz has at least some segment where SSB phone is authorized. The emission table in §97.305(c) is the source. If a question asks where SSB may be used above 50 MHz, the answer covers all those bands rather than any single one.

T1B11.x: Technician HF work is capped at 200 watts PEP on the 80, 40, 15 and 10 meter segments. That number is written directly into §97.313(c)(2). Two numbers carry most of the power questions: 200 watts on Technician HF, 1500 watts nearly everywhere else.

T1B12.x: The blanket limit for any amateur station is 1.5 kW PEP, which is 1500 watts, and that is what applies to a Technician above 30 MHz. Section 97.313(a) still requires you to use the minimum power needed, but 1500 watts is the ceiling the exam is asking for.

T1C01.x: Section 97.17(a) states that no new license grant will be issued for Novice or Advanced Class. Five classes still exist on paper and existing holders keep theirs, but the FCC issues only three today: Technician, General, Amateur Extra.

T1C02.x: Any licensed amateur named in an operator or club station grant may apply for a vanity call sign. There is no license class requirement to request one, though which call signs are available to you does depend on your class.

T1C03.x: The rule is a single sentence, and the answer quotes it nearly verbatim: transmissions to a different country are "limited to communications incidental to the purposes of the amateur service and to remarks of a personal character." Look for that phrasing and pick it.

T1C04.x: Your grant has to show an email address the FCC can actually reach you at. Section 97.23 states plainly that undeliverable correspondence may result in revocation of the station license or suspension of the operator license. Keep the address current after any move or provider change.

T1C05.src: FCC sequential call sign system; 47 CFR §97.19
T1C05.x: Group D covers Novice and Technician licensees and uses the 1x3 format: one letter, one numeral, three letters. KF1XXX fits. Count the characters on each choice and take the one shaped 1x3.

T1C06.x: Section 97.5(a)(2) extends your authority to a vessel documented or registered in the United States, and §97.11(a) requires that installing and operating the station be approved by the master of the ship. Both conditions apply: a US-documented vessel, and the master's permission.

T1C07.x: Renewal may be filed starting 90 days before the expiration date. Do not confuse this with the grace period, which is a separate two-year window that only opens after expiration. Ninety days before, two years after.

T1C08.x: The rule is one line: "An amateur service license is normally granted for a 10-year term." Ten years, every class, with no exam to renew.

T1C09.x: Once a license expires you get a two-year filing grace period to apply for renewal. Miss that window and you retake the exams. Pair it with the 90-day figure from T1C07: file 90 days early, or salvage it within 2 years.

T1C10.x: Passing the exam does not put you on the air. Your authority begins when the operator and station license grant appears in the FCC database. Check ULS, and once your call sign is there, transmit.

T1C11.x: The grace period protects your call sign and lets you renew without retesting. It does not authorize transmitting. An expired license is an expired license, so you stay off the air until the renewal grant appears.

T1D01.x: You may work any country except one whose administration has told the ITU it objects to amateur communications with the United States. The objection has to be filed with the ITU, and the FCC publishes the list. Very few countries are on it, but that ITU notification is the test the question is after.

T1D02.x: Section 97.113(b) is blunt: an amateur station "shall not engage in any form of broadcasting." Other one-way transmissions such as beacons, telecommand and brief tuning are allowed where the rules name them. Broadcasting is the one that is always out.

T1D03.x: Encoding to hide meaning is prohibited, with two narrow exceptions. Section 97.211(b) lets a telecommand station send codes to a space station, and §97.215(b) says model craft control signals do not count as obscuring codes. Space stations and model craft: those are the only two.

T1D04.x: Music by phone emission is prohibited except where this section allows it, and the one opening is in §97.113(c): retransmitting manned spacecraft communications, "including incidental music," with prior NASA approval. Music is only ever legal here as a byproduct of that retransmission.

T1D05.x: You may tell other amateurs that gear is available for sale or trade, "provided that such activity is not conducted on a regular basis." Two conditions ride on this answer: it has to be equipment normally used in an amateur station, and it cannot become a routine business.

T1D06.x: Obscene or indecent words or language appear on the prohibited list in §97.113(a)(4) with no exception, no time-of-day allowance, and no band where it becomes acceptable. When a question offers a conditional answer here, the flat prohibition is the right one.

T1D07.x: An auxiliary station carries communications point to point inside a system of cooperating amateur stations. A link feeding a remote receiver back to the main repeater transmitter is the textbook case. Section 97.201(b) restricts auxiliary stations to 2 meters and shorter.

T1D08.x: Pay for operating is barred except in a few listed cases. The one here: a control operator may accept compensation "as an incident of a teaching position" when the station is used as part of classroom instruction at an educational institution. Teacher, classroom, part of instruction.

T1D09.x: Amateurs may not support program production or news gathering, with one carve-out: communications "directly related to the immediate safety of human life or the protection of property" where no other means is reasonably available at the time. Safety of life or property is the phrase to match.

T1D10.x: The definition is short: "Broadcasting. Transmissions intended for reception by the general public, either direct or relayed." Intent and audience decide it. Whether anyone actually listens does not matter, and neither does the mode.

T1D11.x: Telecommand of model craft is the exception to identifying. Section 97.215(a) drops the identification requirement for transmissions directed only to the model, provided a label with your call sign and address is fixed to the transmitter. Note also §97.215(c): 1 watt maximum.

T1D12.x: There is no such thing as an anonymous test transmission. Section 97.119(a) applies to everything you put on the air, so identify with your assigned call sign even when you are only checking an antenna or setting drive level.

T1E01.x: Section 97.7 opens with it: "When transmitting, each amateur station must have a control operator." There is no exception anywhere in Part 97, including automatic control, where the control operator simply does not have to be at the control point. The answer is never.

T1E02.x: Satellite work follows the same rule as everything else. If your license class authorizes the uplink frequency, you may be the control operator; if it does not, you may not. Check the uplink against your privileges and the question answers itself.

T1E03.x: The station licensee designates the control operator. The FCC presumes the licensee is also the control operator unless station records document otherwise, which is why that presumption is worth remembering alongside this answer.

T1E04.x: Privileges follow the control operator's license class, not the station owner's and not the equipment's. An Extra may operate a Technician's station across Extra segments, and a Technician at an Extra's station is still held to Technician limits.

T1E05.x: Definition, word for word: "Control point. The location at which the control operator function is performed." It is where the operator does the controlling, which may be nowhere near the transmitter.

T1E06.x: Frequency privileges come from the control operator's license class, and no provision lets a Technician work an Extra-only segment. Not with an Extra present, not with permission, not for a special event. The answer is at no time.

T1E07.x: When the two are different people, §97.103(a) makes "both persons equally responsible" for proper operation. Responsibility is shared rather than transferred, so the answer naming both the control operator and the station licensee is the one.

T1E08.x: Automatic control means the station complies with the rules without a control operator present at the control point. A repeater is the everyday example, and §97.205(d) specifically authorizes repeaters to be automatically controlled.

T1E09.x: Section 97.109(c) is one line: "When a station is being remotely controlled, the control operator must be at the control point. Any station may be remotely controlled." Any station. Remote control carries no eligibility restriction, unlike automatic control.

T1E10.x: Remote control is defined as a control operator who "indirectly manipulates the operating adjustments in the station through a control link." The internet is simply one kind of control link. You are still operating the radio yourself, just from somewhere else.

T1E11.x: Straight from the definitions: a control operator is "an amateur operator designated by the licensee of a station to be responsible for the transmissions from that station to assure compliance with the FCC Rules." Designated by the licensee, responsible for compliance.

T1F01.x: The station licensee "must make the station and the station records available for inspection upon request by an FCC representative." No warrant, no advance notice, and no set hours in the rule. Upon request is the standard.

T1F02.x: Tactical calls like Race Headquarters or Net Control are fine for traffic handling, but they satisfy nothing legally. Your FCC-assigned call sign still has to go out at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of it.

T1F03.x: The identification requirement is at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of each one. Note what is not required: you do not have to identify at the beginning. Ten minutes and at the end.

T1F04.x: Identification by phone must be "by a phone emission in the English language." You may hold the entire rest of the contact in any language you like. The call sign itself goes out in English.

T1F05.x: A station running phone may identify by voice or by sending CW. Both are authorized under §97.119(b), and CW is permitted on any frequency the control operator may use. Look for the answer that allows either one.

T1F06.x: Self-assigned indicators are allowed as long as they do not conflict with an indicator specified elsewhere in the rules or with a prefix assigned to another country. Common ones like /M, /P and /AG all qualify, which is why the inclusive answer is correct.

T1F07.x: Third-party traffic with a foreign station requires a third-party agreement between the United States and that country, with an exception for emergency and disaster relief. Absent an agreement or an emergency, the unlicensed person cannot speak.

T1F08.x: The definition names all three parties: a message from the control operator of one amateur station (first party) to the control operator of another (second party) on behalf of another person (third party). Count the parties in each choice and pick the one with all three.

T1F09.x: Definition: "Repeater. An amateur station that simultaneously retransmits the transmission of another amateur station on a different channel or channels." Simultaneously and on a different channel are what separate a repeater from a store-and-forward digipeater.

T1F10.x: Section 97.205(g) protects the repeater operator: the control operator of a repeater that inadvertently retransmits violative communications "is not accountable" for them. Accountability stays with whoever put the signal into the input, which is the originating station.

T1F11.x: A club station license needs at least four members and a trustee who holds an operator license. Four is the number the exam wants. The trustee is designated by a club officer and must be a licensed amateur.

T2A01.x: Standard 2-meter repeater offset is 600 kHz, plus or minus depending on where in the band the output sits. Your radio usually picks the direction automatically. Pair it with the 70 cm figure: 600 kHz on 2 meters, 5 MHz on 70 centimeters.

T2A02.x: 146.520 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency, the channel to try when you want a direct contact without a repeater. It shows up on the Technician exam more than once, so commit the number.

T2A03.x: On 70 centimeters the standard offset is 5 MHz. The band is far wider than 2 meters, so a larger split is practical and keeps the repeater's own transmitter from desensing its receiver.

T2A04.x: Give the other station's call sign, then your own. That is all a repeater contact needs. Long CQ calls are for HF; on a repeater people are monitoring and a short directed call gets answered faster.

T2A05.x: Answer with their call sign first, then yours. Their call tells them you are replying to them rather than to someone else who called at the same moment, and your call tells them who you are.

T2A06.x: Repeat CQ a few times, say "this is," give your call sign, then stop and listen. The rhythm matters: calling too long means you are transmitting while someone is trying to answer you.

T2A07.x: Offset is the difference between the repeater's transmit and receive frequencies. The repeater listens on one and talks on the other, and your radio shifts by the same amount in the opposite direction so the pair line up.

T2A08.src: ITU-R Rec. M.1172; ARRL Operating Manual
T2A08.x: CQ means calling any station. It is a general invitation to anyone listening rather than a call to a particular operator. When you want one specific station, use their call sign instead.

T2A09.x: Give your call sign followed by "listening." It tells the repeater's users that you are there and available without committing them to answer. Shorter and less intrusive than calling CQ, which is why it is the convention on FM.

T2A10.x: A band plan is voluntary. It divides a band by mode and activity so weak-signal work, FM, satellites and digital modes stay out of each other's way. The FCC does not enforce it, but ignoring it counts against good amateur practice under §97.101(a).

T2A11.x: Simplex means transmitting and receiving on one frequency, talking directly to the other station with no repeater in between. Duplex is the opposite, with separate transmit and receive frequencies.

T2B01.x: Reverse swaps your transmit and receive frequencies so you hear the repeater's input instead of its output. Use it to find out whether you can hear the other station directly. If you can, you both might move to simplex and leave the repeater free.

T2B02.x: CTCSS stands for Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System, a low-frequency tone sent under your voice that tells the repeater the signal is meant for it. Motorola's trade name PL is the same thing. The tone sits below the audio passband, so you never hear it.

T2B03.x: In a linked network, whatever one repeater receives goes out on all of them. That extends coverage across a region, so a handheld in one city can reach someone hundreds of miles away through the chain.

T2B04.x: Hearing a repeater does not mean it can hear you. The usual causes are a wrong or missing CTCSS tone, an incorrect offset, or simply being too far away for your low-power signal to reach the input. All three are common, so the inclusive answer is right.

T2B05.src: TIA-603 deviation limits; FM modulation theory
T2B05.x: FM deviation follows your audio level, so talking too loudly drives deviation past what the system allows. The transmitter's limiter clamps the peaks and the receiver loses them, which sounds like your audio cutting out exactly when you get emphatic. Back off the mic.

T2B06.x: DTMF is Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency, the same tones a telephone keypad produces. Each button sends two tones at once, one from a row group and one from a column group, and the pair identifies the digit unambiguously.

T2B07.x: Program the group's ID into your radio. A talkgroup is a numeric identifier rather than a frequency, so joining one is a configuration change, not a tuning change. You stay on the same repeater channel either way.

T2B08.x: Part 97 settles this: licensees and control operators "must cooperate in selecting transmitting channels," and "no frequency will be assigned for the exclusive use of any station." Nobody owns a frequency, so the two stations work it out between themselves.

T2B09.x: Simplex channels give stations close enough to hear each other directly a place to go. A repeater covers a wide area, so two people a mile apart holding a long conversation through one blocks everybody else for no benefit.

T2B10.x: QRM is interference from other stations. Its partner QRN is natural noise such as static from lightning. Keep them straight: QRM is people, QRN is nature.

T2B11.x: QSY means changing frequency. As a question it asks whether you should change; as a statement it announces that you are. Do not confuse it with QSL, which is acknowledgment of receipt.

T2B12.x: The color code is a 4-bit access value carried in every DMR burst. Your radio's programmed code must match the repeater's or it will be ignored. It performs the same job for DMR that a CTCSS tone does for FM, keeping nearby systems on the same frequency from triggering each other.

T2B13.src: ARRL Operating Manual; FM receiver design
T2B13.x: Squelch mutes the receiver audio until a signal appears, sparing you a constant hiss between transmissions. Set it just past the point where the noise stops. Crank it higher than that and weak stations will not break through.

T2B14.x: A talkgroup is a numeric identifier that sorts traffic on a shared digital system. Your radio only unmutes for the groups you have selected, so a single repeater carries many conversations while each user hears only the ones they signed up for.

T2C01.x: Part 97 applies at all times, with no exception for emergencies, drills or field operations. Sections 97.403 and 97.405 do not suspend the rules; they permit any means of radiocommunication when life or property is in immediate danger. Everything else still stands.

T2C02.x: Net control calls the net to order and directs who transmits and when. On a busy net a dozen stations may need to pass traffic, and without one station deciding the order, everyone doubles and nothing moves.

T2C03.x: Spell the word using the standard phonetic alphabet: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie. Unusual names and street addresses are exactly where a listener's brain fills in the wrong word, and phonetics remove the guess.

T2C04.x: RACES is the Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service, defined in Part 97 subpart E for civil defense communications during a national, regional or local emergency. It runs on amateur frequencies but under the direction of a civil defense organization.

T2C05.x: Traffic means formal messages passed between stations, typically radiograms with a set format. It is the business the net exists to move, as distinct from the conversation around it.

T2C06.x: ARES is made up of licensed amateurs who have registered their skills and equipment with the ARRL for public service work. Membership is voluntary and open to any licensee willing to serve, with no government certification involved.

T2C07.x: Transmit only when net control directs you to, unless you have an emergency. That single discipline is what separates a net from a pile-up. A genuine emergency always overrides the order of business.

T2C08.x: Winlink moves email over radio using addresses built from amateur call signs. It lets stations exchange messages with the regular internet when local connectivity is gone, which is why it turns up in emergency work.

T2C09.x: Yes, but only when human life or property is in immediate danger. Section 97.403 permits "any means of radiocommunication at its disposal" in that situation. It is a genuine emergency provision, not a convenience, and it does not cover drills.

T2C10.src: ARRL National Traffic System radiogram format
T2C10.x: The preamble carries the handling data: message number, precedence, station of origin, check, place of origin, and time and date filed. None of it is the message itself. It is what lets any station in the chain track and account for the traffic.

T2C11.src: ARRL National Traffic System radiogram format
T2C11.x: Check is the count of words or word equivalents in the text. The receiving operator counts what they wrote down and compares. If the numbers disagree, something was lost or added and the message gets repeated.

T2C12.x: RACES is the one requiring certification. No station may transmit in RACES unless it is certified by a civil defense organization as registered with that organization. ARES asks only that you volunteer; RACES needs the served agency to enroll you first.

T3A01.src: ITU-R Rec. P.1406; ARRL Antenna Book
T3A01.x: Your signal arrives by several paths at once, direct plus reflections off buildings and terrain. Those copies add or cancel depending on how their phases line up. At 2 meters a half wavelength is about a foot, so moving the antenna a few feet swings you from a null into a peak.

T3A02.x: Leaves and wet wood absorb RF, and the effect climbs sharply with frequency. At UHF and microwave a stand of trees can eat enough signal to drop a marginal path entirely. Strong signals survive; weak ones do not.

T3A03.x: Weak-signal CW and SSB work above 50 MHz is horizontally polarized by convention. FM and repeaters use vertical. Mixing the two costs you signal, so match whatever the activity you are joining uses.

T3A04.x: An antenna responds to the component of the field aligned with it. Cross-polarize the two ends of a line-of-sight path and much of the energy is simply not coupled, typically costing 20 dB or more. The signal weakens rather than disappearing.

T3A05.x: VHF and UHF reflect well off buildings, water towers and hillsides. If the direct path is blocked, swing the beam off-axis and hunt for a surface that bounces you in. Aiming away from the repeater to work it feels wrong and often works.

T3A06.x: Picket fencing is the rapid flutter you hear from a moving vehicle. The car passes through multipath peaks and nulls in quick succession, chopping the signal at a rate that sounds like running a stick along a fence.

T3A07.x: Above roughly 10 GHz, raindrops are a meaningful fraction of a wavelength and scatter and absorb the signal. Heavy precipitation can cut a microwave path badly. The same rain does essentially nothing at HF or VHF.

T3A08.src: ARRL Antenna Book; ITU-R Rec. P.533
T3A08.x: Ionospheric signals reach you by more than one route, often with slightly different path lengths that shift as the layers move. Those copies drift in and out of phase, so the sum rises and falls irregularly. Same physics as VHF multipath, just on a far larger scale.

T3A09.x: The ionosphere twists the polarization of a passing wave, and what comes out is elliptical with a component in nearly every orientation. Because some energy is always available to either orientation, vertical or horizontal antennas both work on HF skip.

T3A10.src: ITU-R Rec. P.1406; digital communications theory
T3A10.x: Delayed copies of the signal smear one symbol into the next, which is intersymbol interference. The receiver starts misreading bits and the error rate climbs. It is why data modes struggle on paths that voice tolerates.

T3A11.x: The ionosphere, roughly 50 to 400 km up, where solar radiation strips electrons from gas atoms. Those free electrons bend HF waves back toward Earth. Strictly it is refraction rather than reflection, though the exam and everyday usage both say reflect.

T3A12.x: Little effect. At 28 and 50 MHz the wavelength is meters long while raindrops are millimeters, far too small to scatter the wave meaningfully. Weather only starts mattering to signal strength up in the microwave bands.

T3B01.x: The electric and magnetic fields sit at right angles to each other, and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel. That geometry falls straight out of Maxwell's equations and holds for every electromagnetic wave.

T3B02.x: Polarization is defined by the orientation of the electric field. Vertical electric field means a vertically polarized wave. The magnetic field is always perpendicular to it, so naming one fixes the other.

T3B03.x: An electric field and a magnetic field, each regenerating the other as the wave travels. Neither exists alone in a propagating wave, which is exactly why it is called electromagnetic.

T3B04.x: Radio waves are light, so they travel at c, about 300,000,000 meters per second in free space. Nothing about being invisible makes them slower. In coaxial cable the speed drops, which is what velocity factor accounts for.

T3B05.x: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related through c = f times lambda. Since c is fixed, raising frequency shortens wavelength. That is why 2 meters is a much higher frequency than 80 meters.

T3B06.x: Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in MHz. The 300 comes from the speed of light expressed as 300 million meters per second divided by a million. Check it: 300 over 146 MHz is about 2 meters.

T3B07.x: Amateur bands carry a wavelength nickname alongside their frequency range. The 146 MHz band is 2 meters, 28 MHz is 10 meters, and so on. Run 300 divided by the frequency and the band name appears.

T3B08.x: Part 97 defines it outright: "VHF (very high frequency). The frequency range 30-300 MHz." The 2-meter and 6-meter bands both live here. Each band above it starts where the last one ends, at ten times the frequency.

T3B09.x: From the same definitions list: "UHF (ultra high frequency). The frequency range 300-3000 MHz." That covers the 70-centimeter band. Note the decade pattern: HF 3 to 30 MHz, VHF 30 to 300, UHF 300 to 3000.

T3B10.x: "HF (high frequency). The frequency range 3-30 MHz." This is the skip territory, holding 80 through 10 meters. Learn the three ranges as one chain and all three questions come free.

T3B11.x: About 300,000,000 meters per second, which is 3 times 10 to the eighth. The precise figure is 299,792,458 m/s, and rounding to 300 million is what makes the 300 divided by frequency shortcut work.

T3B12.x: They all travel at the same speed. In free space c does not depend on frequency, so a 1.8 MHz signal and a 10 GHz signal arrive together. Frequency changes wavelength, never velocity.

T3C01.x: UHF passes straight through the ionosphere instead of bending back down. Without that return path you are limited to what the horizon allows, so a simplex UHF contact ends where line of sight does.

T3C02.x: HF signals refract off the ionosphere and come back to Earth hundreds or thousands of miles away. That skip is routine on HF and rare above it, which is the main practical difference between the two.

T3C03.x: Aurora scatters VHF signals off rapidly moving, uneven curtains of ionized gas. The constant motion Doppler-smears the signal, leaving CW with a rough buzz and SSB barely intelligible. That raspy sound is the giveaway.

T3C04.x: Sporadic E is the usual explanation for sudden strong openings on 10, 6 and 2 meters. Dense patches form in the E region around 60 miles up and reflect signals well above the frequencies the ionosphere normally returns. They come and go without warning.

T3C05.x: A wave passing a sharp edge such as a ridgeline or a building corner bends slightly around it and re-radiates into the shadow behind. Knife-edge diffraction is why a station tucked behind a hill can still be workable.

T3C06.x: Tropospheric ducting traps VHF and UHF signals in a layer of the lower atmosphere that guides them like a waveguide. Paths of 300 miles or more open up, most often over water and in stable weather.

T3C07.x: Six meters is the sweet spot for meteor scatter. Lower frequencies suffer too much ordinary ionospheric interference, higher ones reflect poorly off the brief ionized trails. Bursts last from a fraction of a second to a few seconds.

T3C08.x: A temperature inversion puts warm air above cool air, reversing the normal gradient. The sharp change in refractive index at that boundary bends signals back down instead of letting them escape, forming the duct.

T3C09.src: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center; ARRL Handbook
T3C09.x: Ten meters via the F region works from dawn until shortly after sunset, and only when sunspot numbers are high. The band depends on solar ultraviolet to ionize the F layer enough to bend 28 MHz, so it usually closes after dark.

T3C10.src: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center; ARRL Handbook
T3C10.x: At solar maximum the F region ionizes strongly enough to return 10 meters and sometimes even 6. Both bands go quiet at the bottom of the cycle. The sunspot count is what decides whether they open.

T3C11.src: ITU-R Rec. P.834 (4/3 Earth radius model)
T3C11.x: Air density falls with altitude, so a radio wave bends gently downward as it travels, following the curve of the Earth a little way past where light would leave. Engineers model it as a 4/3 Earth radius, putting the radio horizon roughly 15 percent farther out.

T4A01.x: Mobile gear runs on a nominal 13.8 volts, matching a car's charging system rather than the 12 V battery label. A 50-watt final is only about half efficient, so it pulls near 150 watts from the supply. Divide by 13.8 and you land around 11 amps, which is why 12 A is the sensible rating.

T4A02.x: An SWR meter is built for a frequency range and a power range, and it reads wrong outside either. A meter made for HF will not measure 440 MHz, and a QRP meter reading 100 watts may be damaged. Match both to your station.

T4A03.x: At 12 amps even a small wire resistance costs real voltage, because the drop is current times resistance. Long or thin wire starves the radio on transmit peaks, which shows up as low power or a reset. Short and thick keeps the resistance negligible.

T4A04.x: FT8 is generated and decoded in software, so the radio's audio output feeds the computer's input and the computer's output feeds the radio's mic input. The sound card does the modulating and demodulating; the radio just moves the audio to and from RF.

T4A05.x: Put it in the feed line between transmitter and antenna, because that is the only place the forward and reflected power actually exist. A meter anywhere else is not measuring what reaches the antenna.

T4A06.x: Three signals: audio out of the radio into the computer, audio out of the computer into the radio, and a keying line to switch the transmitter on. Two audio paths and one control line. Modern USB interfaces bundle all three into one cable.

T4A07.x: Receive audio flows from the transceiver's speaker or headphone jack into the computer's line input. That is the path the decoding software listens on. The return path runs the other way, computer output into the radio's microphone or accessory input.

T4A08.x: RF current rides on the surface of a conductor rather than through its middle, so what matters is surface area and low inductance, not cross-sectional area. Flat strap gives you far more perimeter and less inductance per foot than round wire of the same weight.

T4A09.x: Ampere-hours divided by amps leaves hours. A 20 Ah battery feeding a 2 A load runs about 10 hours on paper. Real batteries deliver less under heavy load and in the cold, so treat the figure as an upper bound.

T4A10.x: A hotspot is a low-power digital transceiver that bridges your handheld to a digital voice network over your internet connection. It covers your house, not your county. The reach comes from the network, not from RF.

T4A11.x: Run the negative lead back to the battery's chassis ground rather than picking up a convenient sheet metal screw. Body panels are joined by welds and bolts that make poor, noisy RF connections, and the resulting voltage drop shows up as alternator whine in your audio.

T4A12.x: An electronic keyer turns paddle movements into properly timed dots and dashes at a set speed. You still send the code yourself; the keyer handles the timing so the character spacing stays even.

T4B01.x: Too much microphone gain drives the transmitter past its linear range, so the output no longer follows the input. The result is distorted audio and splatter onto neighboring frequencies. Set gain by ALC indication rather than by ear.
