T4B02.x: Either the keypad or the VFO knob will do it. Direct entry gets you to a known frequency instantly; the knob is for tuning around and finding what is there. Most radios offer both because the two tasks are different.

T4B03.x: Squelch mutes audio below a threshold, so a weak signal that fails to cross it never reaches the speaker. Back the control off until the receiver hisses continuously and the weak station comes through. You trade quiet for sensitivity.

T4B04.x: An FM detector converts frequency shifts to audio using a response curve centered on the carrier. Tune slightly off and the signal sits on a nonlinear part of that curve, so the recovered audio comes out distorted.

T4B05.x: Scanning steps the receiver through a range of frequencies or memory channels, pausing when it finds a signal that breaks squelch. It is how you find activity without turning the knob yourself.

T4B06.x: RIT, also labeled Clarifier, shifts your receive frequency slightly without moving your transmit frequency. Voice pitch on SSB depends on how closely the two stations are tuned, so a small nudge brings a high or low sounding voice back to natural.

T4B07.x: A code plug is the configuration file loaded into a DMR radio: channels, frequencies, color codes, talkgroups and contacts. Nothing works until it is programmed, which is why DMR users trade code plugs for their local systems.

T4B08.x: Noise arrives across the whole passband while the signal occupies only part of it, so a filter matched to the mode admits the signal and rejects the rest. CW needs a few hundred hertz, SSB a couple of kilohertz. Using the right one is often worth more than more antenna.

T4B09.x: Enter the group's identification code. A DMR talkgroup is a number rather than a frequency, so selecting one is a matter of telling the radio which ID to unmute for. Everyone stays on the same channel.

T4B10.x: Communications-quality SSB voice occupies roughly 2.4 kHz, so a 2400 Hz filter passes the intelligence and rejects everything else. Go wider and you let in noise you do not need; go much narrower and the voice starts sounding muffled.

T4B11.x: D-STAR sends your call sign as digital data in every transmission, so the radio must be programmed with it before it will transmit properly. The network uses that call sign for routing, which is why it is not optional the way a memory label is.

T5A01.x: Current is measured in amperes, usually shortened to amps. One ampere is a specific number of electrons flowing past a point each second. In Ohm's law it is the letter I, which trips people up until you have seen it a few times.

T5A02.x: Power is measured in watts. One watt is one joule of energy per second, which is why power always describes a rate rather than an amount. Volts times amps gives you watts in a DC circuit.

T5A03.x: Electron flow through a circuit is called current. Think of the three basics as a set: voltage pushes, current flows, resistance opposes.

T5A04.x: Frequency is the count of complete cycles per second. One cycle takes the waveform positive, back through zero, negative, and back to the start. Sixty cycles per second is 60 hertz.

T5A05.x: A difference in voltage, also called potential difference, is what makes electrons move. No difference means no flow, no matter how good the conductor. Voltage is the push behind the current.

T5A06.x: The hertz, named for Heinrich Hertz, who first demonstrated radio waves. One hertz is one cycle per second, so 7 MHz means seven million cycles every second.

T5A07.x: Metal atoms hold their outermost electrons loosely, leaving a sea of free electrons that drift when voltage is applied. Insulators bind their electrons tightly, so nothing moves. Free electrons are what conduction requires.

T5A08.x: Glass holds its electrons tightly and conducts essentially nothing, which is why it appears in antenna standoffs and high-voltage insulators. Metals do the opposite.

T5A09.x: Alternating current reverses direction repeatedly, flowing one way then the other. Direct current keeps going the same way. House wiring and radio signals are AC; a battery supplies DC.

T5A10.x: Power is the rate at which energy gets used, measured in watts. Energy is the total consumed over time. Your radio draws 100 watts of power; running it an hour consumes 100 watt-hours of energy.

T5A11.x: Resistance opposes both AC and DC alike. A 50-ohm resistor is 50 ohms either way. Reactance, from capacitors and inductors, is the property that behaves differently with AC, and it is not the same thing as resistance.

T5B01.x: Milli means one thousandth, so multiply by 1000 going from amperes to milliamperes: 1.5 A is 1500 mA. Moving to a smaller unit always makes the number bigger.

T5B02.x: Kilo means a thousand, so divide by 1000: 1,500,000 Hz becomes 1500 kHz. Divide again and you get 1.5 MHz, which is the same frequency written a third way.

T5B03.x: Kilo is a thousand, so a kilovolt is 1000 volts. The same prefix works everywhere: kilohertz, kilowatt, kilometer all mean a thousand of the base unit.

T5B04.x: Micro means one millionth, so a microvolt is one millionth of a volt. That is the scale of signals arriving at your receiver's antenna terminals, which is why receiver sensitivity is quoted in microvolts.

T5B05.x: Milli is one thousandth, so divide by 1000: 500 mW is 0.5 watts. Handheld radios on low power and QRP rigs live in this range.

T5B06.x: Divide milliamperes by 1000 to reach amperes: 3000 mA is 3 A. Same conversion as T5B01, run the other direction.

T5B07.x: Multiply MHz by 1000 to get kHz: 3.525 MHz is 3525 kHz. This one is worth knowing cold, since 3.525 MHz is the bottom of the Technician CW segment on 80 meters.

T5B08.x: Pico is a trillionth and micro is a millionth, six decimal places apart. So a million picofarads makes 1 microfarad. Capacitor values run small enough that pF and uF are the units you actually see.

T5B09.x: Doubling power is always 3 dB, whatever the starting point. 5 to 10 watts is a doubling, so 3 dB. Worth memorizing alongside its opposite: halving power is minus 3 dB.

T5B10.x: From 12 to 3 watts is one quarter the power, which is two halvings. Each halving costs 3 dB, so the total is minus 6 dB. The minus sign matters, since power went down.

T5B11.x: A ten times change is 10 dB, so 20 to 200 watts is 10 dB. Two rules cover nearly every decibel question on this exam: doubling is 3 dB, ten times is 10 dB.

T5B12.x: Divide kHz by 1000 to reach MHz: 28400 kHz is 28.400 MHz. That frequency sits in the Technician phone segment on 10 meters, between 28.300 and 28.500.

T5B13.x: Giga is a billion, so divide MHz by 1000: 2425 MHz is 2.425 GHz. This lands in the 13-centimeter band, shared with Wi-Fi and microwave ovens.

T5C01.x: Capacitance is the ability to store energy in an electric field, which a capacitor does between two plates separated by an insulator. Its partner is inductance, which stores energy in a magnetic field instead.

T5C02.x: The farad, named for Michael Faraday. A full farad is enormous, so practical parts are marked in microfarads or picofarads.

T5C03.x: Inductance stores energy in a magnetic field, which is what a coil of wire does when current flows through it. Electric field means capacitance; magnetic field means inductance.

T5C04.x: The henry, named for Joseph Henry. Like the farad it is a large unit, so you will see millihenries and microhenries on real components.

T5C05.x: Impedance is measured in ohms, the same unit as resistance, because both describe opposition to current. That shared unit is why a 50-ohm feed line matches a 50-ohm antenna.

T5C06.x: kHz, with a lowercase k and a capital H. The capital H honors Hertz as a person's name, and SI uses a small k for kilo. Case is not decorative here.

T5C07.x: MHz, capital M and capital H. The capital M distinguishes mega from milli, which uses a lowercase m. Mixing them up changes the value by a factor of a billion.

T5C08.x: Power equals current times voltage, P = I x E. The PIE memory wheel holds all three arrangements: cover P and you get I times E, cover I and you get P over E.

T5C09.x: Multiply volts by amps: 13.8 x 10 = 138 watts. This is the everyday case of a mobile radio on a 13.8-volt supply, so the numbers are worth recognizing.

T5C10.x: 12 volts times 2.5 amperes gives 30 watts. Straight multiplication, no rearranging needed when the question hands you both volts and amps.

T5C11.x: Rearrange P = I x E into I = P / E, then divide: 120 watts over 12 volts is 10 amperes. When the question gives you power and asks for current, divide by the voltage.

T5C12.x: Impedance is the total opposition to alternating current, combining plain resistance with reactance from capacitance and inductance. Reactance varies with frequency, which is why impedance does too.

T5D01.x: I = E / R. Current equals voltage divided by resistance. The Ohm's law triangle has E on top with I and R below, so covering the quantity you want shows the arithmetic.

T5D02.x: E = I x R. Voltage equals current times resistance. With E on top of the triangle, the two below multiply together.

T5D03.x: R = E / I. Resistance equals voltage divided by current. All three forms are the same equation rearranged, so learning the triangle once covers every version.

T5D04.x: Resistance wanted, so divide voltage by current: 90 volts over 3 amperes is 30 ohms. Sanity check by working backward, since 3 amps through 30 ohms does give 90 volts.

T5D05.x: 12 volts divided by 1.5 amperes gives 8 ohms. Fractional currents make people reach for a calculator, but 12 over 1.5 is the same as 24 over 3.

T5D06.x: Divide 12 volts by 4 amperes for 3 ohms. Note the phrasing: drawing 4 amperes from a 12-volt source is the same information as 12 volts across the circuit.

T5D07.x: Current wanted, so divide voltage by resistance: 120 over 80 is 1.5 amperes. When the answer lands between whole numbers, that is usually a sign you divided in the right order.

T5D08.x: 200 volts across 100 ohms gives 2 amperes. Connected across simply means the full voltage appears at the resistor's terminals.

T5D09.x: 240 volts over 24 ohms is 10 amperes. The tidy numbers here make it a good place to check that you are dividing volts by ohms rather than the reverse.

T5D10.x: Voltage wanted, so multiply: 0.5 amperes times 2 ohms is 1 volt. Small currents through small resistances produce small voltages, which is the sanity check on this one.

T5D11.x: 1 ampere through 10 ohms gives 10 volts. Multiplying by one keeps this simple, and it makes the pattern for the next question obvious.

T5D12.x: 2 amperes through 10 ohms is 20 volts. Same resistor as T5D11 with twice the current, so twice the voltage. That proportionality is Ohm's law in one line.

T5D13.x: Series. One path means every electron passes through every component, so the current is identical everywhere. What differs in a series circuit is the voltage across each part.

T5D14.x: Parallel. Each branch connects to the same two points, so each sees the same voltage. Current divides among the branches according to their resistances. Series shares current, parallel shares voltage.

T6A01.x: A resistor opposes current, and how strongly is its resistance in ohms. It is the component you add when a circuit would otherwise pass more current than something downstream can survive.

T6A02.x: A potentiometer is a resistor with a movable contact that taps somewhere along its element. Turning the shaft moves that tap, which is why it works as a volume control. Same part, different name: a variable resistor.

T6A03.x: Resistance. The wiper slides along a resistive track, changing how much of that track sits in the circuit. Everything else follows from that, since changing resistance is what changes the voltage or current you are adjusting.

T6A04.x: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between two plates. Its partner is the inductor, which stores energy magnetically. Electric field means capacitor, every time.

T6A05.x: Two conductive surfaces separated by an insulator is the physical description of a capacitor. The insulator is called the dielectric, and no current flows through it. Energy is held in the field across the gap.

T6A06.x: An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field. Current through a wire creates that field, and winding the wire into a coil concentrates it. Magnetic field means inductor.

T6A07.x: An inductor is literally a coil of wire, sometimes wound on a core to strengthen the field. That coiled shape is exactly how it is drawn on a schematic, which makes it one of the easier symbols to recognize.

T6A08.x: Read the name as a description. Single-pole means one common input; double-throw means it can connect to either of two outputs. So one circuit gets routed to one of two destinations.

T6A09.x: Component 3 shows two terminals with a single hinged lever between them. One contact in, one contact out, one moving arm, so single-pole single-throw. A double-throw switch would show a second contact for the lever to reach.

T6A10.x: Nickel-metal hydride, lithium-ion and lead-acid are all rechargeable, so the inclusive answer is right. These are the chemistries in handhelds, battery packs and station backup supplies precisely because they can be cycled.

T6A11.x: Carbon-zinc is the classic disposable cell, and its chemical reaction does not usefully reverse. Trying to charge one risks leaking or rupturing it. It is the odd one out among the chemistries this pool asks about.

T6B01.x: Forward voltage depends on the semiconductor material. Ordinary silicon diodes drop about 0.7 volts, germanium closer to 0.3, and Schottky types lower still. Since it varies by type, the answer that says so is correct.

T6B02.x: A diode conducts in one direction and blocks the other. That one-way behavior is what makes rectifiers possible, turning alternating current into current that flows only one way.

T6B03.x: A transistor works as a switch when driven hard between fully off and fully on. A small base or gate current controls a much larger current, with no moving parts and switching speeds no mechanical switch can touch.

T6B04.x: A bipolar transistor is three regions of doped semiconductor, either NPN or PNP. The three regions give it its three leads, and the thin middle region is what lets a small current control a large one.

T6B05.x: Gate, drain and source belong to the field-effect transistor. A bipolar transistor uses emitter, base and collector instead. Learn the two sets as pairs and either question gives you the other.

T6B06.x: A stripe on the body marks the cathode end. On the schematic symbol the cathode is the bar the triangle points into, so the painted stripe matches the drawn bar. Conventional current flows into the triangle and out past the stripe.

T6B07.x: Forward current makes an LED light. Electrons crossing the junction release their energy as photons instead of heat, and the semiconductor material sets the color. Reverse the polarity and it simply stays dark.

T6B08.x: Field Effect Transistor. The name describes how it works: voltage on the gate creates an electric field that widens or pinches the channel current flows through. The gate draws almost no current, unlike a bipolar transistor's base.

T6B09.x: Anode and cathode. Current enters at the anode and leaves at the cathode when the diode is forward biased. The cathode is the striped end on the part and the bar on the symbol.

T6B10.x: A transistor provides power gain, using a small input signal to control a much larger output drawn from the power supply. Transformers can raise voltage but never add power. Only an active device with a supply behind it can.

T6B11.x: Gain describes any increase the amplifier produces, whether in voltage, current or power. All three are legitimate ways to express it, so the inclusive answer is correct. Which one matters depends on the job the stage is doing.

T6B12.x: Emitter, base and collector. The base is the thin control region in the middle; current flows between emitter and collector under its command. Pair this with the FET set of gate, drain and source.

T6C01.x: A schematic uses standard symbols to show what is connected to what. It is not a picture of the physical layout, which is why the same schematic can describe boards that look nothing alike.

T6C02.x: Component 1 is drawn as a sharp zigzag in the signal path, which is the standard resistor symbol. Here it sits between the input terminals and the transistor's base, limiting the current that reaches it.

T6C03.x: Component 2 is a circle containing a vertical bar with two angled leads, one carrying an arrowhead. That is a bipolar transistor. The bar is the base, and the arrow marks the emitter and tells you it is an NPN.

T6C04.x: Component 3 is the small dome or loop shape at the top of the drawing, the standard symbol for a lamp. It sits in the transistor's collector circuit, so the transistor switching on is what lights it.

T6C05.x: Component 4 is the stack of alternating long and short parallel lines, which is the battery symbol. The long line is positive and the short one negative. More pairs of lines simply suggest more cells.

T6C06.x: Component 6 is two parallel plates with one side curved, the symbol for a capacitor. It sits from the rectifier output to ground, which is the classic filter position where it smooths the pulsating DC.

T6C07.x: Component 8 is a diode triangle with two small arrows pointing away from it. Those arrows mean the junction emits light, making it a light emitting diode. Arrows pointing toward the symbol instead would mean a photodiode.

T6C08.x: Component 9 is a resistor zigzag with an arrow touching it, which marks an adjustable tap along the element. That makes it a variable resistor. The same symbol with three connected terminals is a potentiometer.

T6C09.x: Component 4 is two coils drawn facing each other with lines between them representing the core. That is a transformer, and here it takes the AC input down to a lower voltage before the rectifier.

T6C10.x: Component 3 is a coil with an arrow tapping it. Coil means inductor, and the arrow means adjustable, so it is a variable inductor. The same arrow convention marks the variable capacitors elsewhere in this figure.

T6C11.x: Component 4 is the triangle at the top right, the standard antenna symbol. It sits at the output end of the tuned network, which is exactly where the antenna belongs in a matching circuit.

T6C12.x: A schematic accurately shows component connections and nothing more. It does not tell you where parts sit on the board, how long the wires are, or what anything physically looks like. Connections are the whole point.

T6D01.x: A rectifier passes current in one direction only, so an AC input comes out as DC that varies but never reverses. Adding a filter capacitor after it smooths that pulsating output into something steady.

T6D02.x: A relay is a switch operated by an electromagnet rather than by hand. A small control current pulls the contacts closed, letting a low-power circuit switch a much larger one while keeping the two electrically separate.

T6D03.x: Shielding wraps a grounded conductor around the signal wire so stray fields terminate on the shield instead of the conductor inside. It blocks interference in both directions, keeping noise out and your signal in.

T6D04.x: A meter displays an electrical quantity as a number, whether on a digital readout or a moving pointer against a scale. The quantity depends on what you set it to measure.

T6D05.x: A regulator holds output voltage steady as the input voltage or the load current changes. Without one, your radio would see the supply sag every time the transmitter keyed up.

T6D06.x: A transformer changes AC voltage using two coils sharing a magnetic field. The turns ratio sets the change, so fewer turns on the secondary gives a lower voltage. It only works on AC, since a changing field is what couples the coils.

T6D07.x: LEDs are the standard visual indicator: low current, long life, and no filament to burn out. That is why the front panel of every modern radio is covered in them.

T6D08.x: A capacitor combined with an inductor forms a resonant circuit. Their opposing reactances cancel at one frequency, and that frequency is where the circuit responds most strongly. It is the basis of every filter and tuned stage in your radio.

T6D09.x: An integrated circuit packs many semiconductors and other components onto one chip. It is how a function that once filled a chassis now fits in a package smaller than your fingernail.

T6D10.x: Component 2 is the transistor, and its job in this circuit is controlling current. A small current into the base governs the much larger current flowing through the lamp, so the transistor acts as the switch or amplifier.

T6D11.x: An inductor and a capacitor together, wired in series or in parallel. Either arrangement resonates, though they behave oppositely at that frequency: series presents minimum impedance, parallel presents maximum.

T7A01.x: Sensitivity is how weak a signal the receiver can still detect, usually quoted in microvolts. Its partner term is selectivity, which is about separating signals rather than hearing faint ones. Detect means sensitivity.

T7A02.x: A transceiver is a receiver and transmitter in one box, sharing circuitry such as the VFO and often the filters. The word itself is the two terms fused together.

T7A03.x: A mixer combines two frequencies and produces their sum and difference, which is how a signal gets shifted to another frequency. It is the heart of every superheterodyne receiver, converting incoming signals down to a fixed intermediate frequency.

T7A04.x: Selectivity is the ability to separate a wanted signal from others nearby, and it comes mostly from the receiver's filters. Sensitivity hears the weak one; selectivity ignores the loud neighbor.

T7A05.x: An oscillator generates a signal at a chosen frequency, converting DC from the supply into AC at radio frequency. Every transmitter and receiver contains at least one, since without a generated reference there is nothing to mix against.

T7A06.x: A transverter shifts a transceiver's whole operating range onto another band, converting both transmit and receive. It lets an HF radio work a microwave band without replacing the radio, which is common practice on the higher bands.

T7A07.x: PTT means push to talk, and grounding that input switches the radio from receive to transmit. A foot switch, a microphone button, or a computer interface all work the same way: connect the line to ground and the transmitter keys.

T7A08.x: Modulation is impressing information onto a carrier by varying one of its properties. Change the amplitude and you get AM, the frequency and you get FM. Speech plus carrier equals modulation.

T7A09.x: SSB and CW-FM place different demands on an amplifier. SSB is a varying envelope needing linear amplification, while FM and CW have constant amplitude and can tolerate more efficient nonlinear operation. The switch sets the amplifier up correctly for the mode you picked.

T7A10.x: An RF power amplifier raises the transmitter's output, taking a few watts in and producing many more using energy from its own supply. Remember §97.313(a) still applies: use the minimum power needed.

T7A11.x: The VFO sets the frequency you transmit and receive on, and it is what moves when you turn the tuning knob. Variable is the operative word, distinguishing it from a crystal oscillator locked to one frequency.

T7B01.x: Over-deviation means your audio is driving the transmitter past its allowed frequency swing, which splatters into adjacent channels and sounds distorted. Backing away from the microphone lowers the audio level and brings deviation back in range.

T7B02.x: The fault is usually in the consumer receiver, not your transmitter. Broadcast sets are built cheaply with poor front-end filtering, so a strong nearby signal on any frequency can overload the input stage. Your signal is legal and on frequency; their radio simply cannot reject it.

T7B03.x: Interference comes from many directions: arcing power lines, switching supplies, LED lighting, and consumer electronics of every kind. Since all the listed sources genuinely cause it, the inclusive answer is right.

T7B04.x: High SWR means power is reflecting back into the transmitter, and solid-state finals protect themselves by folding back output. Low power with everything else normal usually points at the antenna system rather than the radio.

T7B05.x: When a receiver cannot reject your signal, the fix belongs at that receiver. A filter at its antenna input blocks your frequency before it reaches the overloaded front end. Filtering your own transmitter does nothing if your signal is already clean.

T7B06.x: Start by proving your own station is clean. Check that it is working properly and that it does not interfere with your own equipment on the same channel. That tells you whether the problem is yours to fix or theirs, and it is the answer any FCC inquiry would expect.

T7B07.x: A band-reject filter, also called a notch or trap, attenuates the commercial FM broadcast band while passing 2 meters. The broadcast station is legal and strong, so the practical fix is keeping its energy out of your receiver's front end.

T7B08.x: Work through it cooperatively: make sure your own station is clean, then help the neighbor identify the offending device, since consumer gear must accept interference under Part 15. All the listed steps are reasonable, so the inclusive answer is correct.

T7B09.x: Start with the connectors. Loose or improperly installed coax fittings let signal leak in and out, and they are by far the most common cause of cable TV interference. It costs nothing to check and usually solves it.

T7B10.x: Distorted repeater audio has several likely causes: over-deviation from talking too loudly, RF getting back into the microphone circuit, or simply operating too far from the repeater. All are genuine, so the inclusive answer is right.

T7B11.x: A clip-on ferrite choke adds impedance to common-mode RF riding on the microphone cable, stopping your own transmitted signal from feeding back into the audio stages. That feedback is a classic cause of distorted transmit audio in a high-RF shack.

T7C01.x: A dummy load absorbs your output so you can test and tune without radiating. It lets you key up, check power and adjust settings without occupying a frequency or interfering with anyone.

T7C02.x: An antenna analyzer sweeps a range of frequencies and shows SWR or impedance across it, so you can see where the antenna is actually resonant. An SWR meter tells you the situation at one frequency while transmitting; the analyzer maps the whole picture without transmitting.

T7C03.x: A 50-ohm non-inductive resistor on a heat sink. Fifty ohms matches normal feed line, non-inductive keeps the impedance flat across frequency, and the heat sink handles the power, since every watt you send becomes heat.

T7C04.x: A 1:1 reading means no reflected power, so the load impedance matches the line exactly. SWR is a ratio and 1:1 is the ideal floor. It can never read below that.

T7C05.x: Reflected power from a mismatch stresses the output transistors with voltage and current they were not designed for. Solid-state finals have no tolerance for it, so the radio reduces power to protect them. Tube amplifiers were far more forgiving, which is why this behavior surprises older operators.

T7C06.x: Any SWR above 1:1 indicates a mismatch between feed line and antenna, and 4:1 is a substantial one. The number tells you the degree of mismatch, not what caused it, so it could be the antenna, the feed line, or a connector.

T7C07.x: Lost power becomes heat in the conductors and the dielectric. It does not radiate and it does not come back. That is why a long run of lossy cable at UHF can waste more power than the radio delivers to the antenna.

T7C08.x: A directional wattmeter measures forward and reflected power separately, and SWR follows directly from their ratio. Many meters do that calculation for you and show SWR on the scale.

T7C09.x: Moisture is the usual killer. Water wicks into the braid and dielectric, raising loss and corroding the shield, and the damage travels well beyond the entry point. Sealing connectors properly is the cheapest maintenance you can do.

T7C10.x: Sunlight breaks down the polymer jacket over time, leaving it cracked and brittle. Once cracked it admits water, and moisture is what actually ruins the cable. UV resistance protects the jacket so the jacket can protect the coax.

T7C11.src: Transmission line theory; ARRL Antenna Book
T7C11.x: Foam dielectric has less loss per foot because much of the insulation is air, which absorbs far less RF energy than solid polyethylene. The tradeoff is that foam is easier to crush and lets moisture migrate more readily if the jacket is breached.

T7D01.x: A voltmeter measures electric potential, or the difference in potential between two points. Potential is the formal name for what everyone calls voltage.

T7D02.x: In parallel, across the component. Voltage is a difference between two points, so you need probes on both sides of the part you are measuring. A voltmeter has very high resistance so it barely disturbs the circuit while connected.

T7D03.x: In series, so the current you want to measure actually flows through the meter. That means breaking the circuit to insert it. An ammeter has very low resistance, which is why connecting one across a voltage source is a good way to destroy it.

T7D04.x: An ammeter measures current, and it goes in series with the circuit. The name comes from ampere, the unit it reads.

T7D05.x: An ohmmeter supplies a small known current from its own battery, measures the voltage that results, and applies Ohm's law to report resistance. That is why it needs power of its own and why the circuit under test must be unpowered.

T7D06.x: The resistance setting expects the meter to supply the current, not receive it. Apply an external voltage in that mode and you push current through circuitry never designed for it, often taking out the meter or its fuse.

T7D07.x: A multimeter reads voltage and resistance, and nearly all of them read current too. The name says it: multiple measurements in one instrument.

T7D08.x: Acid-core solder is made for plumbing. Its flux is corrosive and stays active after the joint cools, quietly eating the connection and nearby traces. Electronics work uses rosin-core solder instead.

T7D09.x: A cold joint looks dull, rough or lumpy rather than smooth and shiny. It formed without enough heat for the solder to flow and wet the metal properly, so it may test fine today and fail intermittently later. Reheat it until it flows.

T7D10.x: The ohmmeter's own small current charges the capacitor. As charge builds, the voltage across it rises and the meter interprets that as rising resistance, climbing toward infinity. Watching that behavior is a rough way to check whether a large capacitor is healthy.

T7D11.x: Power the circuit down first. An ohmmeter works by injecting its own current, so any external voltage corrupts the reading and can damage the meter. Discharge any large capacitors before probing, too.

T8A01.x: SSB is amplitude modulation with the carrier and one sideband removed. All the information rode in the sidebands anyway, so stripping the rest saves bandwidth and power without losing anything. It remains AM at heart.

T8A02.x: VHF packet feeds its tones through an ordinary FM radio, so the modulation is FM or PM. The packet gear generates audio tones and the radio treats them like any other audio, which is why a standard 2-meter rig works unmodified.

T8A03.x: SSB is the weak-signal voice mode above 50 MHz. Its narrow bandwidth concentrates your power and lets the receiver use a tight filter, so contacts stay workable at signal levels where FM would deliver nothing but hiss.

T8A04.x: Repeaters use FM or PM. FM's constant amplitude survives multipath and noise well, and its capture effect means the strongest signal takes the channel cleanly instead of two stations garbling each other.

T8A05.x: CW is the narrowest of these, needing only about 150 Hz. There is no voice content to carry, just a carrier switched on and off, so the occupied bandwidth comes down to the keying speed.

T8A06.x: Upper sideband is the convention on 10 meters and everything above. Lower sideband is used on 160, 80 and 40 meters. The dividing line falls at 10 meters, so remember 20 meters and up is USB along with all of VHF and UHF.

T8A07.x: SSB occupies roughly 3 kHz against 10 to 15 kHz for FM voice. Narrower bandwidth means your transmitter power is concentrated and the receiver can filter more tightly, which is why SSB reaches farther on the same watts.

T8A08.x: About 3 kHz, which is roughly the range of frequencies that carry intelligible speech. That figure anchors several others worth knowing: the 2.8 kHz limit on 60 meters and the 2400 Hz receiver filter that gives the best signal-to-noise ratio.

T8A09.x: Between 10 and 15 kHz. FM spreads energy across a band several times wider than the audio it carries, which is the price of its noise immunity. That is also why repeater channels are spaced 15 or 20 kHz apart.

T8A10.x: About 6 MHz, the same width as a broadcast television channel. Moving full-motion video in real time takes roughly two thousand times the bandwidth of an SSB voice signal.

T8A11.x: Roughly 150 Hz. Keying a carrier on and off creates sidebands proportional to the keying speed, so at normal code speeds the signal stays very narrow. That narrowness is why CW gets through when nothing else will.

T8A12.x: FM's capture effect means the receiver locks onto the strongest signal and suppresses everything else, so you hear one station at a time. On SSB two stations on nearly the same frequency both come through, which is sometimes an advantage and sometimes a mess.

T8B01.x: Beacons carry telemetry about the satellite itself: battery voltage, temperatures, and the state of its systems. Ground stations track that data to know whether the spacecraft is healthy and which transponder is active.

T8B02.x: A linear transponder shares its limited output power among every signal passing through it. Running too much uplink power captures a disproportionate share and pushes everyone else down into the noise. It is the satellite equivalent of shouting over a conversation.

T8B03.x: Tracking software gives you when the satellite rises and sets, where to point the antenna in azimuth and elevation, and how much Doppler shift to expect. All of the listed outputs are standard, so the inclusive answer is correct.

T8B04.x: Amateur satellites carry FM, SSB, CW and digital modes depending on the spacecraft. There is no single satellite mode, so the inclusive answer is right. FM birds are the easiest starting point with a handheld and a small beam.

T8B05.x: A beacon is a steady transmission carrying the satellite's status information. It also gives you a reference signal for aiming your antenna and gauging Doppler before you try to work the transponder.

T8B06.x: Keplerian elements are the numbers describing the orbit's size, shape and orientation, distributed as two-line element sets. Feed current elements into tracking software and it computes where the satellite will be. They go stale, so refresh them.

T8B07.x: Relative motion between satellite and ground station shifts the received frequency, high as it approaches and low as it recedes. On a fast low orbit the shift is large enough that you retune continuously through a pass.

T8B08.x: The letters name the bands in order, uplink first. U is 70 centimeters and V is 2 meters, so U/V means you transmit on 70 centimeters and listen on 2 meters. Getting the order backwards is the classic beginner error.

T8B09.x: The satellite tumbles or spins, so its antennas keep changing orientation relative to yours. As the polarization rotates in and out of alignment with your antenna, the signal rises and falls in a regular rhythm.

T8B10.x: Low Earth Orbit, a few hundred kilometers up with a period near 100 minutes. That means fast passes lasting only ten or fifteen minutes, plenty of Doppler, and the need to track the satellite as it crosses.

T8B11.x: Anyone may receive it. Satellite telemetry is transmitted in the clear precisely so that anyone can decode it, and encoding to obscure meaning would run against Part 97 anyway. Listening has never required a license.

T8B12.x: Compare your downlink signal to the satellite's beacon. Matching the beacon means you are using a fair share of the transponder. Louder than the beacon means you are taking more than your share and squeezing out other stations.

T8C01.x: Radio direction finding locates a transmitter by taking bearings from several positions and seeing where they cross. It is the standard method for tracking down noise sources, stuck transmitters and deliberate interference.

T8C02.x: A directional antenna, since the hunt depends on knowing which way the signal is coming from. An omnidirectional antenna hears the transmitter equally from everywhere, which tells you nothing about where to walk.

T8C03.x: Contesting is working as many stations as possible inside a set time. Contacts are brief and formulaic because the goal is volume, which is also why contest operating sounds so different from ordinary conversation.

T8C04.x: Send your call sign and the required exchange, nothing more. Everyone on the band is trying to maximize contacts, so extra conversation costs both operators rate. Brevity is courtesy in a contest.

T8C05.x: A grid locator, or Maidenhead locator, compresses latitude and longitude into a short string such as FN31pr. Two letters, two digits and often two more letters narrow your position to a few kilometers, which is enough for VHF work and awards.

T8C06.x: You send DTMF tones, the same touch-tone digits a telephone keypad produces. The node decodes them as commands to connect to or disconnect from another node, so your radio's keypad becomes the dialing interface.

T8C07.x: Voice over Internet Protocol digitizes speech and carries it as data packets across the internet. Amateur linking systems use it to join distant repeaters, so the RF hop is local at each end and the internet covers the middle.

T8C08.x: IRLP links repeaters and other amateur systems over the internet. Every user is on real RF at their end; the internet only carries audio between nodes, which is why IRLP requires a radio to participate.

T8C09.x: EchoLink allows a computer or smartphone to connect directly into the system without RF at that end. That is the distinction from IRLP, where every participant must be on the air.

T8C10.x: You register your call sign and provide proof of license before the system will admit you. Since EchoLink can key transmitters, it has to verify that everyone connecting is actually licensed.

T8C11.x: A gateway is the station bridging amateur radio and the internet, passing traffic between the two. Winlink gateways and IRLP nodes are both examples of the same idea.

T8D01.x: Packet, PSK31, FT8, RTTY and the rest are all digital modes, so the inclusive answer is right. What they share is encoding information as discrete symbols rather than as a continuously varying analog waveform.

T8D02.x: FT8 is built for signals buried in noise, decoding reliably well below what an ear can hear. It trades speed and flexibility for sensitivity: fixed 15-second transmissions carrying a very small, highly structured message.

T8D03.x: APRS carries position, weather data, short text messages and telemetry. All the listed types are genuine, so the inclusive answer applies. It is a general-purpose data channel that happens to be used mostly for position reporting.

T8D04.x: NTSC is the analog color television standard used in North America before digital broadcasting, and amateurs use it for fast-scan TV. It is analog and full motion, which is what separates it from slow-scan TV.

T8D05.x: APRS plots station positions on a live map, which makes it valuable for public service events where net control needs to see where everyone actually is. Real time and tactical are the words to match.

T8D06.x: Phase Shift Keying. Information is encoded by shifting the carrier's phase rather than its amplitude or frequency. PSK31 uses it to fit a keyboard conversation into about 31 Hz of bandwidth.

T8D07.x: DMR uses two-slot TDMA, interleaving two conversations in alternating time slots on one 12.5 kHz channel. Two independent contacts share the same frequency without hearing each other, which effectively doubles repeater capacity.

T8D08.x: A packet frame carries the sender and destination call signs, the data payload, and a checksum for error detection. All the listed elements are part of the frame, so the inclusive answer is correct.

T8D09.x: CW stands for continuous wave, and Part 97 defines it as international Morse code telegraphy. In practice it means keying a carrier on and off. It remains the narrowest and most power-efficient way to get a message through a bad path.

T8D10.x: WSJT-X supports FT8, FT4, meteor scatter, EME and other weak-signal work, so the inclusive answer is right. The common thread is decoding signals well below the noise floor using known message structure.

T8D11.x: ARQ means Automatic Repeat reQuest. The receiver checks each block for errors and asks for a resend when one fails, so the data arriving is correct rather than merely approximate. The cost is throughput on a poor path.

T8D12.x: Mesh networking runs commercial Wi-Fi hardware on modified firmware, moving it onto amateur frequencies that overlap the Part 15 bands and allowing amateur power levels. It is still an amateur station, so encryption to obscure meaning stays prohibited.

T9A01.x: A beam antenna concentrates radiation in one direction instead of spreading it everywhere. The energy has to come from somewhere, so what it adds in front it takes from the sides and back. Yagis and quads are the common examples.

T9A02.x: Loading inserts an inductor into a radiating element so a physically short antenna behaves electrically like a longer one. It is how a 2-meter-long mobile whip works on 40 meters. The coil buys resonance, not efficiency.

T9A03.x: Antenna polarization is named for the orientation of the electric field it radiates. A vertical element produces a vertical electric field, so it is vertically polarized. Same definition used for the wave itself in T3B02.

T9A04.src: ARRL Antenna Book; antenna efficiency theory
T9A04.x: That short rubber antenna is heavily loaded to resonate in a fraction of the length it needs, and loading raises losses while lowering radiation resistance. Much of your power warms the antenna instead of leaving it. It works, just inefficiently.

T9A05.x: Resonant length and frequency are inversely related, so a shorter dipole resonates higher. Trimming a dipole raises its resonant frequency, which is why you cut antennas long and shorten them in steps.

T9A06.x: Of the usual choices, the Yagi has the most gain. Its driven element plus reflector and directors form an array that reinforces radiation forward and cancels it elsewhere. Adding more directors buys more gain and a narrower beam.

T9A07.x: A vehicle body is a metal box that behaves like a Faraday shield, attenuating signals passing through it. Your handheld inside the car is partly enclosed by that shield, so both transmit and receive suffer. An external antenna solves it.

T9A08.x: At 146 MHz a wavelength is about 2.05 meters, so a quarter wave is near 20 inches. Trim slightly for end effect and you land at 19. You can rebuild that number any time from 300 divided by frequency.

T9A09.x: A 5/8-wave whip concentrates radiation at a lower angle toward the horizon, which is exactly where distant stations are. That lower takeoff angle is the gain, and it matters more for mobile work than raw height ever will.

T9A10.src: ARRL Antenna Book; dipole radiation pattern
T9A10.x: A dipole radiates strongest broadside, at right angles to the wire, and puts nulls off the ends. Point the wire across the path you want rather than at it. The pattern is a doughnut with the antenna through the hole.

T9A11.x: Gain is the increase in signal in a chosen direction compared with a reference antenna, usually a dipole or an isotropic radiator. No antenna creates power. Gain is redistribution, taking from directions you do not need.

T9B01.src: ARRL Antenna Book; connector weatherproofing practice
T9B01.x: Every outdoor connector needs sealing, whichever type it is, so the inclusive answer is right. Water entering a connector wicks into the coax and ruins it well beyond the joint, and that damage is invisible until performance falls off.

T9B02.src: Transmission line theory; ARRL Antenna Book
T9B02.x: Fifty ohms is the amateur standard, and it is what transceivers, meters and dummy loads are built around. The figure is an engineering compromise between the impedances that minimize loss and maximize power handling in coax.

T9B03.x: Coax is popular because it is forgiving. The shield confines the field inside the cable, so you can run it along metal, bury it, or coil it without upsetting the impedance. Open-wire line has lower loss but demands spacing from everything.

T9B04.src: Impedance matching theory; ARRL Antenna Book
T9B04.x: A tuner matches the impedance the antenna system presents to what the transmitter wants to see, usually 50 ohms. Note what it does not do: it changes nothing at the antenna itself, so SWR on the feed line stays exactly where it was.

T9B05.x: Loss rises with frequency. Skin effect crowds current into an ever thinner surface layer as frequency climbs, raising effective resistance, and dielectric losses grow too. A cable that is fine on 40 meters may be wasteful at 440 MHz.

T9B06.x: Type N maintains a constant 50-ohm impedance through the connector and seals well, so it performs properly above 400 MHz. UHF connectors have no controlled impedance, which becomes a real loss at those frequencies despite the name.

T9B07.x: The PL-259, also called the UHF connector, is the familiar screw-on fitting on HF and VHF gear. Its name is historical rather than descriptive: it does not hold a constant impedance, so it is a poor choice at true UHF.

T9B08.x: Loss comes from conductor resistance, dielectric absorption, and radiation or leakage through an imperfect shield. All the listed mechanisms are genuine contributors, so the inclusive answer applies.

T9B09.x: Readings that jump around, especially when the wind blows or you flex the cable, point at a loose or corroded connection rather than a design problem. A steady mismatch reads steady. Intermittent readings mean intermittent contact.

T9B10.x: Both are 50-ohm cable, but RG-213 is much larger, so its bigger conductor and thicker dielectric mean lower loss at any given frequency. That is the electrical difference; the physical one is that RG-58 is far easier to route.

T9B11.src: Transmission line theory; ARRL Antenna Book
T9B11.x: Air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss, because air absorbs almost nothing compared with solid dielectric and the large center conductor has very little resistance. The tradeoffs are cost, weight, and the fact that it barely bends.

T9B12.x: SWR expresses how well the load matches the line, derived from the ratio of forward to reflected power. A perfect match reflects nothing and reads 1:1. The number describes the relationship between line and load, not the quality of either alone.
